metadata.author: Florus of Lyon
known_issues: A few evident corrupt or nonstandard printed readings were translated according to sense and documented in notes, including “mediatorum” for the mediator and “generatione vitis” for the fruit of the vine.
The phrase “in ejusdem laudis persecutione” appears corrupt; I translated the evident sense, “in the continuation of that same praise,” and noted the printed reading.
Several biblical references follow the printed Latin even where the quotation spans additional verses or corresponds to a different numbering tradition; such cases are noted in the relevant chunks.
The opening numbered paragraphs, such as “8.” through “12.”, have been treated as section numbers rather than audio headings, so they are not voiced in the English.
The phrase “regalibus caeremoniis” in chunk 9 is translated literally as “royal ceremonies,” although the context suggests a possible corrupt reading for “legal ceremonies.”
Several printed biblical references appear confused or displaced; they have been spoken exactly as printed in the English, with discrepancies noted in the relevant chunks.
The final sentence of this chunk introduces the Church’s reply but the quoted reply itself occurs in the next chunk.

Several printed scripture citations in this passage give only the first or a selected verse while the quoted text extends across additional verses; the English speaks the printed citations and notes the mismatch in the relevant chunks.
Several Scripture references are cited exactly as printed even where they do not match modern or Vulgate verse numbering; discrepancies are noted in the relevant chunks.
Translation note: The printed Latin has “vinnm,” evidently for “vinum”; it is translated as “wine.”
The opening Sanctus quotation is printed incompletely, without “of your glory”; it has been translated as printed while preserving Florus’s later discussion of the full phrase.
Several printed biblical citations in this passage do not match standard verse divisions; each citation has been spoken as printed, with discrepancies noted locally.

The printed “oblata sunt; et ideo oblata” in chunk 10 appears corrupt for “ablata sunt; et ideo ablata.” The translation gives the evident sense, “taken away,” and records the printed reading in the notes.
The final quotation, “Nothing is impossible for you,” is cited only as Scripture in the Latin, without a book, chapter, or verse.

Several Scripture citations are printed with references that do not match the quoted text: the Gospel of Luke, chapter three, verse thirteen; Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter fourteen, verse twenty-five; and the Gospel of John, chapter five, verse forty-five. Each citation has been spoken as printed and noted locally.
Psalm numbering is rendered according to the printed Latin citation, not adjusted to modern English Bible numbering.
The Isaiah quotation in chunk 52 is translated exactly as printed, even though it differs from the usual biblical wording of Isaiah chapter six, verse three.
A few apparent corrupt readings or typographical errors were translated according to the evident sense and noted in the relevant chunks.
Some printed Scripture references cite only the opening verse of a longer quotation; the English speaks the printed citation and notes the mismatch where it occurs.
The printed phrase “redempta,... ejus non est” in section twenty-five is corrupt or lacunose and has been represented explicitly rather than emended.
Several Scripture citations in the printed Latin do not match modern verse numbering or the apparent biblical source; each citation has been spoken as printed and noted locally.
The opening siglum “ID. ibid.” has been rendered as [Augustine] based on the assumed preceding source; the prior chunk is needed for absolute certainty.
Translation note: Scripture citations are rendered as printed, even where the quoted wording may extend beyond the printed verse reference.
The printed Psalm text in chunk 26 appears to have “ad cum” where the sense requires “ad eum”; this was translated according to the evident sense and noted.
Some biblical quotations are cited imprecisely in the printed Latin; the English speaks the printed citation and explains the issue in the relevant notes.
Several biblical citations are printed in abbreviated or imprecise form; they have been rendered aloud exactly as printed, with discrepancies noted in the relevant chunk notes.

The printed citation “I Cor. XI, 1” attached to “Be imitators of God…” is not the actual biblical source; the quotation corresponds to Paul's letter to the Ephesians, chapter five, verses one through two.
The Hebrews quotations in chunk 9 differ from standard biblical wording in several places; the translation follows the printed Latin rather than harmonizing the text.
The grammatical discussion of “Seraphim” versus “Seraphin” in chunk 55 depends on Latin and Hebrew/Greek word endings; the English preserves the distinction by spelling out the final letters.

corrections.original: At that time, within the mystery, there was not yet the sacrifice
corrections.corrected: This was in mystery, as a figure; there was not yet the sacrifice
corrections.latin: et hoc in mysterio nondum erat sacrificium corporis et sanguinis Domini
corrections.reason: Augustine's point is that the Aaronic sacrifices were a figure ('in mysterio'); the English makes 'mystery' a place in which the Eucharist was absent, which obscures the figure/reality contrast and misuses the key term mysterium.

corrections.original: but when the figure is removed, the truth appears
corrections.corrected: but the figure will be removed, and the truth will appear
corrections.latin: sed tolletur figura, et apparebit veritas
corrections.reason: Future tenses (tolletur, apparebit) rendered as a timeless present; the following question 'when will the veil be removed?' depends on the future.

corrections.original: he will not change this priesthood for any other arrangement
corrections.corrected: he will in no way change this priesthood
corrections.latin: hoc sacerdotium nulla alia ratione mutabit
corrections.reason: 'nulla alia ratione' = 'on no other account / in no way'; 'for any other arrangement' suggests a substitution not in the Latin.

corrections.original: —printed as Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians
corrections.corrected: —Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians
corrections.latin: (I Cor. XI, 1)
corrections.reason: 'printed as' is editorial meta-commentary added to the narrated text; the discrepancy belongs in the notes (it is already there).

corrections.original: In other words, he cleansed us by taking what we were, while not taking what we had become through sin.
corrections.corrected: That is, through what we were and what we were not.
corrections.latin: per hoc scilicet quod eramus et non eramus
corrections.reason: Added interpretive gloss; the Latin only says 'through what we were and were not', which the next two sentences themselves explain.

corrections.original: For the Holy Spirit was pleased that
corrections.corrected: For from that time on the Holy Spirit was pleased that
corrections.latin: Ex hoc enim placuit Spiritui sancto
corrections.reason: 'Ex hoc' (thenceforth) dropped; Augustine's point is that the fasting custom arose after the Last Supper.

corrections.original: This order, which the whole Church throughout the world observes, was arranged by the Apostle himself, and it is not changed by any of these differences.
corrections.corrected: This order, which the whole Church throughout the world observes, is to be understood as arranged by the Apostle himself, in so far as it is not varied by any of these differences.
corrections.latin: ab ipso ordinatum esse, quod nulla horum diversitate variatur
corrections.reason: The relative clause 'quod nulla ... variatur' identifies what was ordered by the Apostle (what is uniform everywhere); the English turns it into an independent assertion that the whole order is unchanged.

corrections.original: from the humility of shared suffering
corrections.corrected: from the lowliness of affliction
corrections.latin: ab humilitate contribulationis
corrections.reason: 'contribulatio' means affliction/tribulation; 'shared' reads the prefix con- as 'together', which the word does not mean.

corrections.original: Among us, he was despised by us. Then he remained with us.
corrections.corrected: Among us he was despised by us, and afterward he was despised along with us.
corrections.latin: et contemptus est inter nos a nobis, et postea nobiscum
corrections.reason: 'nobiscum' continues 'contemptus est' (despised among us, by us, and with us); 'he remained with us' invents a new verb and loses the point that Christ shared our being despised, which the next sentence ('He taught us to accept being despised') builds on.

corrections.original: We must always remember where these words are placed
corrections.corrected: We must always remember where these words come from
corrections.latin: recordari oportet semper haec verba unde sint
corrections.reason: 'unde sint' = whence they are (their source/origin), not their position.

corrections.original: For right thought makes a person devout.
corrections.corrected: For this way of thinking is what makes a person devout.
corrections.latin: quia cogitatio pium facit
corrections.reason: 'cogitatio' refers back to the recognition just described (that any good life is by God's grace); 'right thought' generalizes it into a different claim.

corrections.original: in which the mediator was offered
corrections.corrected: in which the mediator was sacrificed
corrections.latin: per illud singulare sacrificium, in quo mediator est immolatus
corrections.reason: 'immolatus' is the sacrificial slaying, not merely 'offered' (oblatus); keeps sacrificium/immolare distinct from oblatio.

corrections.original: The heavens, the powers of the heavens, and the blessed Seraphim
corrections.corrected: The heavens, the Virtues of the heavens, and the blessed Seraphim
corrections.latin: Coeli coelorumque virtutes
corrections.reason: Florus contrasts 'angeli, dominationes, potestates' with 'coeli, coelorum virtutes, Seraphim'; rendering both potestates and virtutes as 'powers' blurs the two lists in the very sentence that contrasts them. Align with the chunk-54 fix.

corrections.original: the heavens, the powers of the heavens, and the Seraphim also
corrections.corrected: the heavens, the Virtues of the heavens, and the Seraphim also
corrections.latin: sed etiam coeli, et coelorum virtutes, et Seraphim concelebrant
corrections.reason: Same as above: second occurrence in the same chunk, next to 'angels, dominions, and powers' (potestates).

corrections.original: and in their assembly they all rejoice together over him, and over one another in him.
corrections.corrected: and in their assembly they all rejoice with one another.
corrections.latin: vicissim de se omnes in suo conventu gratulantur
corrections.reason: 'over him ... in him' is imported from the later sentence ('de illo, et de se in illo laetantur'); here the Latin says only that they congratulate one another in their assembly.

corrections.original: the Powers are named after the heavens. This name, “Powers,” is sometimes used
corrections.corrected: the Virtues are named after the heavens. This name, “Virtues,” is sometimes used
corrections.latin: post coelos ponuntur Virtutes, quo nomine omnes coelestes spiritus
corrections.reason: In chunk 50 Gregory defines 'Potestates' (English 'Powers') as the order that restrains hostile spirits; here Virtutes are the order through whom miracles are done. Calling both 'Powers' makes the narration contradict itself about what 'the Powers' do. Use the traditional 'Virtues' for the order Virtutes (the Psalm quotations 'all their power' / 'Lord of powers' can stay).

corrections.original: the Powers are those spirits through whom signs and miracles
corrections.corrected: the Virtues are those spirits through whom signs and miracles
corrections.latin: proprie in ordinibus angelorum Virtutes illi spiritus vocantur, per quos signa et miracula frequentius fiunt
corrections.reason: Same Virtutes/Potestates collision as above (second occurrence).

corrections.original: praise, revere, and celebrate
corrections.corrected: praise, tremble before, and celebrate
corrections.latin: majestatem Dei Patris laudare, tremere, et communi exsultatione concelebrare
corrections.reason: 'tremere' is 'tremble', the third of the thematic acts (laudant, adorant, tremunt) developed in chunks 50–52; 'revere' loses it.

corrections.original: and the honor or glory given to the Father is also given to the Son, as the same Son says
corrections.corrected: and honoring the Son is the honor or glory of the Father, as the same Son says
corrections.latin: sic visio Filii Patris est contemplatio, Patris honorificentia sive gloria
corrections.reason: The elliptical Latin parallels the first member (seeing the Son = contemplating the Father): honoring the Son is the Father's honor or glory. The English reverses the direction.

corrections.original: as they praise this hymn of God’s glory
corrections.corrected: as they sing this hymn of God’s glory
corrections.latin: Istae sunt voces angelorum laudantium in coelis hunc hymnum gloriae Dei
corrections.reason: The angels are not praising the hymn; 'laudantium hunc hymnum' = uttering this hymn of praise.

corrections.original: A likeness of the sacrifice was offered to the one to whom the reality itself would later be offered:
corrections.corrected: A likeness was offered to him, promising the reality of the sacrifice—to him to whom the reality itself was to be offered:
corrections.latin: ut ei offerretur similitudo, promittens veritatem sacrificii, cui erat offerenda ipsa reddita veritas

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: The Mass as Mystery and Humility
chunks.latin: DE EXPOSITIONE MISSAE
chunks.english: Exposition of the Mass

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 1. Incipit opusculum de actione missarum collectum quam maxime, et in ordinem digestum ex verbis sanctorum Patrum Cypriani, Ambrosii, Augustini, Hieronymi, Gregorii, Fulgentii, Severiani, Vigilii, Isidori, Bedae, Aviti, sicut suis locis per singula litterae nominum quae forinsecus praenotantur ostendunt; sed et ex antiquis mysteriorum libris quaedam verba necessario sumpta sunt. Quod autem eadem nomina in ipsa opusculi serie ubique inserta non sunt, illa necessitas fecit, ne frequens eorum interpositio fieret absurda et incommoda ipsius dictionis et sensuum interruptio. In qua tamen expositiuncula non tam verba, quae satis simplicia sunt, sed potius ipsius mysterii ratio et actio imponitur et commendatur, videlicet qua fide celebrandum, quanta pie tate sit amplectendum.
chunks.english: Here begins a short work on the action of the Mass. It has been gathered as fully as possible and arranged in order from the words of the holy Fathers: Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Fulgentius, Severian, Vigilius, Isidore, Bede, and Avitus. The letters of their names, marked in the margin at the appropriate places, show which Father is being used in each passage. Some words have also, when necessary, been taken from ancient books of the mysteries. But those same names have not been inserted everywhere into the running text of this little work. Necessity required this, so that constantly interrupting the text with names would not create an awkward and inconvenient break in the wording and in the flow of thought. In this brief explanation, however, what is set forth and commended is not so much the wording, which is quite simple, but rather the meaning and action of the mystery itself: that is, with what faith it must be celebrated, and with how much devotion it must be embraced.
chunks.notes: The column markers have been omitted from the English as editorial apparatus. “Actio” is rendered here as “the action,” in the liturgical sense of the canon or central eucharistic action.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 2. (AUG. in Psal. XXXIII, n. 4.) In mysterio corporis et sanguinis Domini nostri Jesu Christi, quod sancta Ecclesia per universum mundum pro ejusdem mundi salute offert, maxime nobis humilitas commendatur. Viam enim nobis fecit idem Dominus Jesus Christus per humilitatem, quia per superbiam recesseramus a Deo: redire autem ad eum nisi per humilitatem non poteramus, et quem nobis proponeremus ad imitandum non habebamus. Omnis enim mortalitas hominum superbia tumebat, etsi existeret aliquis humilis vir in spiritu, sicut erant prophetae et patriarchae, dedignabatur genus humanum imitari humiles homines. Ne ergo dedignaretur homo imitari hominem humilem, Deus factus est humilis, ut vel sic superbia generis humani non dedignaretur sequi vestigia Dei. Erant autem, ut legimus, sacrificia antea Judaeorum secundum Aaron in victimis pecorum, et hoc in mysterio nondum erat sacrificium corporis et sanguinis Domini, quod nunc diffusum est toto orbe terrarum. Proponamus nobis ergo ante oculos duo sacrificia, et illud secundum ordinem Aaron, et hoc secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Scriptum est enim: «Juravit Dominus, et non poenitebit eum, tu es sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech» (Psal. CIX, 4). Hoc autem manifeste dicitur de Domino nostro Jesu Christo. Quis ergo erat Melchisedech? utique, sicut legimus, rex Salem. Salem civitas fuit antea illa, quae postea, sicut docti prodiderunt, Jerusalem dicta est. Ergo antequam ibi regnarent Judaei, ibi erat ille sacerdos Melchisedech, qui scribitur in Genesi sacerdos Dei excelsi. Ipse occurrit Abrahae, quando liberavit Loth de manibus persequentium, et prostravit eos a quibus ille feriebatur, et liberavit fratrem. Post liberationem fratris occurrit ei Melchisedech. Tantus erat Melchisedech a quo benediceretur Abraham. Protulit panem et vinnm et benedixit Abraham, et dedit ei decimas Abraham. Vide quid protulit et quem benedixit, et dictum est postea: «Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech.» David hoc in spiritu dixit longe post Abraham. Temporibus autem Abrahae fuit Melchisedech. De quo ergo alio dicit: «Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem» «Melchisedech,» nisi de illo cujus novimus sacrificium?
chunks.english:
[Augustine] In the mystery of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the holy Church offers throughout the whole world for that same world’s salvation, humility is especially commended to us. For the Lord Jesus Christ himself made a way for us through humility, because through pride we had withdrawn from God. We could not return to God except through humility, and we had no one set before us whom we could imitate. All mortal humanity was swollen with pride. And even if there was some man humble in spirit, as the prophets and patriarchs were, the human race disdained to imitate humble human beings. Therefore, so that a human being would not disdain to imitate a humble human being, God became humble. In this way, at least, the pride of the human race would not disdain to follow the footsteps of God.

Now, as we read, the earlier sacrifices of the Jews, according to Aaron, consisted in animal victims. This was in mystery, as a figure; there was not yet the sacrifice of the body and blood of the Lord, which has now been spread throughout the whole world. So let us place two sacrifices before our eyes: that one according to the order of Aaron, and this one according to the order of Melchizedek. For Scripture says, “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: you are a priest according to the order of Melchizedek,” in Psalm one hundred nine, verse four. This is clearly said about our Lord Jesus Christ.

Who, then, was Melchizedek? Surely, as we read, he was the king of Salem. Salem was the earlier name of that city which, as learned writers have handed down, was afterward called Jerusalem. Therefore, before the Jews reigned there, that priest Melchizedek was there, the one written of in Genesis as the priest of the Most High God. He met Abraham when Abraham had rescued Lot from the hands of his pursuers, struck down those by whom Lot was being attacked, and freed his kinsman. After this rescue of his kinsman, Melchizedek met Abraham. So great was Melchizedek that Abraham was blessed by him. He brought out bread and wine, and he blessed Abraham; and Abraham gave him tithes. Notice what he brought out, and whom he blessed. And afterward it was said, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” David said this in the Spirit long after Abraham. But Melchizedek lived in the time of Abraham. About whom else, then, does he say, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” except about the one whose sacrifice we know?
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: “(AUG. in Psal. XXXIII, n. 4.)”. The siglum is rendered only as “[Augustine]” according to the work-specific instruction. The Scripture citation “(Psal. CIX, 4)” is rendered as printed: Psalm one hundred nine, verse four. The printed Latin reads “vinnm”; translated as “wine,” taking it as “vinum.” “Brother” in the Latin refers to Lot as Abraham’s kinsman.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 3. Sublatum est enim sacrificium Aaron, et coepit esse sacrificium secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Dominus itaque noster Jesus Christus in corpore et sanguine suo voluit esse salutem nostram. Unde autem commendavit corpus et sanguinem suum? De humilitate sua. Nisi enim esset humilis, nec manducaretur, nec biberetur. Respice altitudinem ipsius: «In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum» (Joan. I, 1). Ecce cibus sempiternus; sed manducant angeli, manducant sempiternae virtutes, manducant coelestes spiritus, et manducant et saginantur, et integrum manet quod eos satiat et laetificat. Quid autem homo posset ad illum cibum? Unde cor tam idoneum illi cibo? Oportebat ergo, ut mensa illa lactesceret, et ad parvulos perveniret. Unde autem fit cibus lac? Unde cibus in lac convertitur, nisi per carnem trajiciatur? Nam mater hoc facit; quod manducat mater, hoc manducat infans; sed quia minus idoneus est infans qui pane vescatur, ipsum panem mater incarnat, et utilitate mamillae et lactis succo de ipso pane pascit infantem. Quomodo ergo de ipso pane pavit nos sapientia Dei? Quia «Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis» (Joan. I, 14). Vide ergo humilitatem, quia panem angelorum manducat homo. Et scriptum est: «Panem coeli dedit eis, panem angelorum manducavit homo» (Psal. LXXVII, 24), id est Verbum illud quo pascuntur angeli sempiternum, quod est aequale Patri, manducavit homo, quia «cum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse se aequalem Deo» (Phil. II, 6). Saginantur illo angeli; sed «semetipsum exinanivit,» ut manducaret panem angelorum homo, «formam servi accipiens in similitudine hominum factus, et habitu inventus ut homo. Humiliavit se, factus obediens usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis,» ut jam de cruce commendaretur nobis caro et sanguis Domini novum sacrificium.
chunks.english:
For the sacrifice of Aaron has been taken away, and the sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek has begun. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ willed that our salvation should be in his body and blood. But from what did he commend his body and blood to us? From his humility. For unless he were humble, he would not be eaten, and he would not be drunk.

Look at his height: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” in the Gospel of John, chapter one, verse one. Behold the eternal food. But the angels eat it; the everlasting powers eat it; the heavenly spirits eat it. They eat and are filled, and yet what fills and gladdens them remains whole and undiminished. But what could a human being do with that food? Where would the human heart come from that was fit for such food? That table, then, had to become like milk and reach little children.

But how does food become milk? How is food turned into milk, unless it passes through flesh? That is what a mother does. What the mother eats, the infant eats. But because the infant is not yet capable of feeding on bread, the mother, so to speak, embodies that bread; and by the service of the breast, and through the liquid nourishment of milk, she feeds the infant from that very bread. So how did the Wisdom of God feed us from that bread itself? Because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” in the Gospel of John, chapter one, verse fourteen.

See, then, the humility: a human being eats the bread of angels. And Scripture says, “He gave them the bread of heaven; a human being ate the bread of angels,” in Psalm seventy-seven, verse twenty-four. That is, the eternal Word by which the angels are fed, the Word equal to the Father, was eaten by a human being, because, “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized,” in Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two, verse six. The angels are filled by him; but “he emptied himself,” so that a human being might eat the bread of angels, “taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross”—so that from the cross itself the flesh and blood of the Lord might now be commended to us as the new sacrifice.
chunks.notes: The citation “(Psal. LXXVII, 24)” is rendered as printed: Psalm seventy-seven, verse twenty-four. In the Vulgate, the wording “a human being ate the bread of angels” is commonly associated with the following verse as well; the printed reference has not been changed. The Philippians quotation continues beyond the printed citation “(Phil. II, 6),” but no additional citation is printed in the source.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 4. (AUG. in Psal. LXIV, 1.) Ipse ergo a Domino Deo missus sacerdos noster, assumpsit a nobis quid offerret Deo. Illas sanctas primitias carnis ex utero Virginis holocaustum obtulit Deo: extendit manus [Col. 0018A] in cruce, ut diceret: «Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo, elevatio manuum mearum sacrificium vespertinum» (Psal. CXL, 2), sicut novimus, quia Dominus circa vesperam pependit in cruce, et impietates nostrae propitiatae sunt; alioquin absorbuerant nos. Merito illi cantavimus in psalmo: «Et impietates nostras tu propitiabis» (Psal. LXIV, 4). Tu sacerdos, tu victima, tu oblator, tu oblatio. Ipse sacerdos est, qui nunc ingressus est interiora veli. Solus ibi ex his qui carnem gestaverunt interpellat pro nobis. In cujus rei figura in illo primo populo, et in illo primo templo, unus sacerdos intrabat in Sancta sanctorum (Heb. IX, 7), populus omnis foris stabat, et ille qui solus ingrediebatur interiora veli, offerebat sacrificium pro populo [Col. 0018B] foris stante. Quid enim ageretur in illo populo Judaei nescierunt; sed modo sciunt; de illis quippe dictum est: «Quandiu legitur Moyses, velamen supra cor eorum positum est, ibi velamen figura est; sed tolletur figura, et apparebit veritas» (II Cor. III, 15). Sed quando tolletur velamen? audi Apostolum: «Cum autem transiens ad Dominum auferetur velamen» (Ibid., vers. 16). Propitiatis ergo peccatis nostris et impietatibus per illud sacrificium vespertinum, transimus ad Dominum, et auferetur velamen Propterea et Domino crucifixo velum templi scissum est.
chunks.english: [Augustine] Therefore, he himself, our priest sent by the Lord God, took from us what he would offer to God. He offered to God, as a whole burnt offering, those holy firstfruits of flesh taken from the womb of the Virgin. He stretched out his hands on the cross, so that he could say, as Scripture says in Psalm one hundred forty, verse two: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands, like the evening sacrifice.” For we know that the Lord hung on the cross toward evening, and our sins were atoned for; otherwise they would have swallowed us up. Rightly, then, we sang to him in the psalm, Psalm sixty-four, verse four: “And you will atone for our sins.” You are the priest; you are the victim; you are the one who offers; you are the offering. He is the priest who has now entered behind the inner veil. There, he alone, of all who have borne flesh, intercedes for us. As a figure of this, among that first people and in that first temple, one priest entered the Holy of Holies, as described in the Letter to the Hebrews, chapter nine, verse seven. All the people stood outside, while the one man who entered behind the inner veil offered sacrifice for the people standing outside. The Jews did not understand what was taking place among that people; yet now they know. For it was said about them, in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter three, verse fifteen: “As long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” There, the veil is the figure; but the figure will be removed, and the truth will appear. And when will the veil be removed? Listen to the Apostle, in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter three, verse sixteen: “But when someone passes over to the Lord, the veil will be removed.” So, once our sins and acts of ungodliness have been atoned for through that evening sacrifice, we pass over to the Lord, and the veil is removed. That is why, when the Lord was crucified, the veil of the temple was torn.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(AUG. in Psal. LXIV, 1.)”. The initial “4.” is treated as an editorial section number and is not spoken. Scripture citations have been rendered in spoken form. The phrase “sed modo sciunt” is translated as printed, though the surrounding argument stresses the veil over Jewish understanding.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Itaque nec carnem praeputii circumcidimus juxta ritum Mosaicae legis, nec abstinemus carnibus, quas eadem lex dicit immundas, nec sabbata et neomenias et dies festos eorum carnaliter observamus, [Col. 0018C] nec victimas pecorum sacrificamus Deo, nec pascha in ove et azymis similiter celebramus, et si qua alia fuerunt vetera sacramenta, quae omnia umbras futurorum appellat Apostolus, quia ea significabant suo tempore revelanda quae nos revelata percipimus, ut remota umbra nuda eorum luce frueremur. Nam et exuendo veterem hominem circumcidimur in exspoliatione corporis carnis, et quos cibos illi vetant in pecoribus, nos vitamus in moribus, et exhibemus corpora nostra hostiam vivam, sanctam, Deo placentem, cui et animas nostras in desideriis suis pro sanguine intelligenter effundimus, et Christi velut Agni immaculati sanguine ab omni iniquitate mundamur, qui propter similitudinem carnis peccati etiam caprino pecore in [Col. 0018D] veteribus sacrificiis figuratur, nec eum negat in crucis carnibus taurum, qui in illo cognoscit maximam victimam. In illo requiem cum invenimus, vere sabbatizamus, et lunae novae observatio vitae novae est sanctificatio, et pascha nostrum est Christus, et azymus noster sinceritas veritatis, fermentum non habens vetustatis; et quaecunque alia illis veteribus adumbrata sunt signis, in isto habent finem, cujus regni non erit finis.
chunks.english: And so we do not circumcise the flesh of the foreskin according to the rite of the Mosaic law. We do not abstain from the meats that the same law calls unclean. We do not keep their Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days in a merely bodily way. We do not sacrifice animal victims to God. We do not celebrate Passover in the same way, with a lamb and unleavened bread. And the same applies to any other ancient sacraments there were. The Apostle calls all of them “shadows of things to come,” because they pointed toward realities that were to be revealed in their own time, realities that we now receive as already revealed. The shadow has been removed, so that we may enjoy their unveiled light. For by putting off the old humanity, we are circumcised in the stripping away of the body of flesh. The foods they forbid among animals, we avoid in our behavior. We present our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. To him we pour out our souls with all their desires in place of blood, understanding this in a spiritual sense. We are cleansed from every sin by the blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb. Because he came “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” he was also prefigured in the old sacrifices by the goat; and anyone who recognizes in him the greatest victim does not refuse to see him, in the flesh of the cross, as the bull as well. When we find rest in him, we truly keep Sabbath. The observance of the new moon is now the sanctification of a new life. Our Passover is Christ, and our unleavened bread is the sincerity of truth, with no leaven of oldness. Whatever else was foreshadowed by those ancient signs finds its fulfillment in him, whose kingdom will have no end.
chunks.notes: Biblical phrases such as “shadows of things to come,” “living sacrifice,” “likeness of sinful flesh,” and “our Passover is Christ” are translated as scriptural allusions; no explicit citations are printed in the source at these points.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: In illo quippe omnia oportebat impleri, qui venit legem et prophetas non solvere, sed implere. Proinde illa vetera signa rerum non evacuavit arguendo, sed implendo mutavit, ut alia essent quae nuntiarent venisse jam Christum, [Col. 0019A] quam fuerant illa quae praenuntiabant esse venturum. Quoniam ergo sicut scriptum est in Cantico canticorum, «aspiravit dies» (Cant. II, 17), removeantur umbrae; spiritualis significatio jam lucescat, carnalis celebratio jam quiescat, audiamus Dominum vetera Judaeorum sacrificia repudiantem, et novum Christi sacrificium apertissime promittentem per Malachiam prophetam dicentem: «Non est mihi voluntas in vobis, dicit Dominus, et munus non suscipiam de manu vestra. Ab ortu enim solis usque ad occasum magnum est nomen meum in gentibus, et in omni loco sacrificatur, et offertur nomini meo oblatio munda, quia nomen meum magnum est in gentibus, dicit Dominus exercituum» (Malach. I, 10). Certe hic negare non possunt Judaei, non solum non accipere [Col. 0019B] sacrificium de manibus eorum, sed nec se illi offerre manibus suis. Locus enim unus est lege Domini constitutus, ubi manibus eorum sacrificia jussit offerre, praeter quem locum omnino prohibuit. Hunc ergo locum quem pro suis meritis amiserunt, etiam sacrificium quod ibi tantum licebat offerri in locis aliis offerre non audent. Ecce omnimodo impletum est, quod ait propheta, «Et munus non suscipiam de manibus vestris.»
chunks.english: For everything had to be fulfilled in him who came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill them. Therefore, he did not invalidate those old signs by condemning them; he changed them by fulfilling them. There had to be one set of signs to announce that Christ had now come, just as there had been another set of signs to announce beforehand that he was going to come. So, as it is written in the Song of Songs, chapter two, verse seventeen, “the day has dawned.” Let the shadows be removed. Let the spiritual meaning now shine out. Let the bodily celebration now come to rest. Let us hear the Lord rejecting the old sacrifices of the Jews and, through the prophet Malachi, very openly promising the new sacrifice of Christ. He says, in the book of Malachi, chapter one, verse ten: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not receive a gift from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place sacrifice is offered, and a clean offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts.” Surely the Jews cannot deny this: not only does God not receive sacrifice from their hands, but they themselves no longer offer it to him with their hands. For the law of the Lord established one place where he commanded sacrifices to be offered by their hands, and he absolutely forbade them to be offered anywhere else. They lost that place because of their own deserts; and since the sacrifice was allowed to be offered only there, they do not dare offer it in other places. See, then, how completely the prophet’s word has been fulfilled: “And I will not receive a gift from your hands.”
chunks.notes: The Malachi citation is printed as chapter one, verse ten, though the quoted material extends into what is commonly numbered verse eleven. The citation is spoken as printed, in accordance with the rule for confused or incomplete references.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Neque hoc ita praedictum et impletum est, ut eos prophetica sententia respondere permittat. Quia manibus non offerimus carnem, corde et ore offerimus laudem, secundum illud in psalmo: «Immola Dei sacrificium laudis etiam» (Psal. XLIX, 14), hinc enim contradicit eis qui dicit: «Non est mihi voluntas mea in vobis.» Deinde ne existiment Judaei, [Col. 0019C] quod illis non offerentibus, nec illo accipiente de manibus eorum Deo, sacrificium non offeratur, quo quidem ille non eget, qui bonorum nostrorum nullius indiget: tamen quia sine sacrificio non est, quod non illi, sed nobis utile est, audiant ipsum Dominum contestantem, imo aperiant oculos et videant, quia «ab ortu solis usque ad occasum,» non in uno, sicut in illis fuerat constitutum, sed «in omni loco» offertur sacrificium Christianorum, nec cuilibet Deo, sed ei qui ista praedixit Deo Israel. Unde alibi dicit Ecclesiae suae: «Et Redemptor tuus Deus Israel, Deus universae terrae vocabitur» (Isa. LIV, 5). Hoc sacrificium mundum offertur Deo Israel, non ab una gente Judaeorum, de cujus manibus non se accepturum praedixit, sed ab omnibus gentibus, quae dicant: [Col. 0019D] «Venite, ascendamus ad montem Domini,» nec in uno loco sicut praeceptum erat in terrena Jerusalem; sed in omni loco usque in ipsam Jerusalem; nec secundum ordinem Aaron, sed secundum ordinem Melchisedech. Christo enim dictum est, et de Christo tantummodo ante praedictum est: «Juravit Dominus et non poenitebit eum: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech» (Psal. CIX, 4). Quid est «juravit Dominus,» nisi inconcussa veritate firmavit? Et quid est «non poenitebit eum,» nisi hoc sacerdotium nulla alia ratione mutabit? neque enim sicut hominem poenitet Deum, sed Dei dicitur poenitentia [Col. 0020A] quaevis ab illo institutae rei cujusque mutatio, quae credebatur esse mansura, proinde cum dicit «non poenitebit eum: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech,» satis ostendit eum poenituisse, hoc est cum mutare voluisse sacerdotium, quod constituerat secundum ordinem Aaron, sicut de utroque videmus impletum. Nam et Aaron sacerdotium jam nullum est in aliquo templo, et Christi sacerdotium aeternum perseverat in coelo.
chunks.english: Nor was this foretold and fulfilled in such a way that the prophetic statement leaves them any answer. They might say, “We do not offer flesh with our hands; we offer praise with heart and mouth,” according to the saying in the psalm, Psalm forty-nine, verse fourteen: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise also.” But the one who says, “I have no pleasure in you,” contradicts them precisely here. Then, so that the Jews may not think that, because they do not offer sacrifice and God does not receive it from their hands, no sacrifice at all is offered—though God certainly does not need sacrifice, since he needs none of our goods—still, because sacrifice is not absent, and because it is useful not to him but to us, let them hear the Lord himself testifying. Better yet, let them open their eyes and see: “from the rising of the sun to its setting,” not in one place as had been established for them, but “in every place,” the sacrifice of Christians is offered. And it is not offered to just any god, but to the one who foretold these things, the God of Israel. Thus he says elsewhere to his Church, in Isaiah, chapter fifty-four, verse five: “And your Redeemer, the God of Israel, will be called the God of the whole earth.” This clean sacrifice is offered to the God of Israel, not by the one nation of the Jews, from whose hands he foretold that he would not receive it, but by all nations, who say, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” It is not offered in one place only, as was commanded in the earthly Jerusalem, but in every place, even in Jerusalem itself. And it is not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek. For it was said to Christ, and foretold in advance about Christ alone, in Psalm one hundred nine, verse four: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” What does “The Lord has sworn” mean, except that he has confirmed it with unshakable truth? And what does “he will not repent” mean, except that he will in no way change this priesthood? God does not repent the way a human being does. Rather, “repentance” is attributed to God when he changes something he had instituted, something people believed would remain. Therefore, when he says, “He will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” he shows clearly that he did repent of the other priesthood—that is, that he chose to change the priesthood he had established according to the order of Aaron. We see both things fulfilled. There is now no priesthood of Aaron in any temple, while the priesthood of Christ endures forever in heaven.
chunks.notes: The wording of Psalm forty-nine, verse fourteen is translated as printed: “Immola Dei sacrificium laudis etiam,” which is somewhat awkward Latin compared with the standard form of the verse. The quotation “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” is printed without a citation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Hunc sacerdotem et hoc sacerdotium magnifice commendat apostolus, cum gratiam Evangelii a regalibus caeremoniis distinguens, scribit ad Hebraeos: «Et alii quidem plures facti sunt sacerdotes, eo quod morte prohiberentur permanere; hic autem eo quod maneat in aeternum, sempiternum habet sacerdotium:»[Col. 0020B] «unde et salvare in perpetuum potest, accedens per semetipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro eis. Talis decebat ut nobis esset pontifex, sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus, et excelsior coelis factus, qui non haberet quotidie necessitatem, quemadmodum sacerdotes, primo pro suis peccatis hostias offerre, deinde pro populi. Hoc enim fecit semel seipsum offerendo» (Hebr. VII, 28). Et iterum: «Talem habemus pontificem, qui consedit ad dextram majestatis in coelis, sanctorum minister et tabernaculi veri quod fecit Deus et homo» (Hebr. VIII, 1).
chunks.english: The Apostle gives magnificent praise to this priest and this priesthood when, distinguishing the grace of the Gospel from the royal ceremonies, he writes to the Hebrews: “And the others were made priests in greater number, because death prevented them from remaining; but he, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood. Therefore he is able to save forever, as he comes to God through himself, always living to intercede for them. It was fitting that we should have such a high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; one who would not have daily need, as the priests do, first to offer victims for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people. For he did this once, by offering himself.” This is cited as the Letter to the Hebrews, chapter seven, verse twenty-eight. And again: “We have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which God and man made.” This is cited as the Letter to the Hebrews, chapter eight, verse one.
chunks.notes: The printed reference “Hebr. VII, 28” does not match the full range of the quotation, which corresponds chiefly to Hebrews chapter seven, verses twenty-three through twenty-seven; the citation is nevertheless spoken as printed. The Latin has “accedens per semetipsum ad Deum,” singular, and is translated as printed rather than harmonized to the usual biblical wording. The phrase “a regalibus caeremoniis” is translated literally as “from the royal ceremonies,” though “legal ceremonies” would better fit the context. The quotation of Hebrews chapter eight, verse one includes the printed phrase “quod fecit Deus et homo,” translated literally as “which God and man made”; this differs from the standard biblical wording.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Sancti ergo patres nostri in Veteri Testamento uni Deo et Creatori omnium victimas obtulerunt, quas sibi ipse offerri voluit, per earum similitudinem promittens victimam veram, per quam nos sibi peccatorum [Col. 0020C] remissione reconciliavit in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, ut ei offerretur similitudo, promittens veritatem sacrificii, cui erat offerenda ipsa reddita veritas in passione corporis et sanguinis Christi. Hujus sacrificii caro et sanguis ante adventum Christi per victimas similitudine promittebatur, in passione Christi per ipsam veritatem reddebatur, post ascensum Christi per sacramentum memoria celebratur. Proinde prima sacramenta, quae observantur et celebrantur ex lege, praenuntiativa erant Christi venturi, quae cum suo adventu Christus implevisset, oblata sunt; et ideo oblata quia impleta, non enim venit solvere legem sed adimplere. Alia sunt instituta virtute majora, utilitate meliora, actu faciliora, numero pauciora, tanquam justitia fidei [Col. 0020D] revelata, et in libertate vocatis filiis Dei jugo servitutis ablato, quod duro et carni dedito populo congruebat, qualia sunt in Ecclesia baptismus Christi, eucharistia Christi, signaculum Christi.
chunks.english: Therefore, our holy fathers in the Old Testament offered victims to the one God, the Creator of all things. God himself willed that these victims be offered to him, and through their likeness he promised the true victim. Through that true victim, in Christ Jesus our Lord, he reconciled us to himself by the forgiveness of sins. A likeness was offered to him, promising the reality of the sacrifice—to him to whom the reality itself was to be offered: the reality given back in the passion of the body and blood of Christ. Before the coming of Christ, the flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised in likeness through sacrificial victims. In the passion of Christ, they were given in the reality itself. After the ascension of Christ, they are celebrated in memory through the sacrament. Therefore the first sacraments, those observed and celebrated according to the law, announced beforehand the Christ who was to come. Once Christ had fulfilled them by his coming, they were taken away; and they were taken away because they had been fulfilled. For he did not come to abolish the law, but to bring it to completion. Other sacraments were then instituted: greater in power, better in benefit, easier in practice, fewer in number. This happened as the righteousness of faith was revealed, as the children of God were called into freedom, and as the yoke of slavery—fitting for a hard people devoted to the flesh—was removed. Such are, in the Church, the baptism of Christ, the eucharist of Christ, and the seal of Christ.
chunks.notes: The printed Latin reads “oblata sunt; et ideo oblata quia impleta,” literally “they were offered; and therefore offered because fulfilled.” The sense and the common theological argument require “ablata sunt; et ideo ablata,” “they were taken away; and therefore taken away.” The translation follows that evident sense and records the printed reading here.  Printed 'oblata sunt; et ideo oblata quia impleta' is an evident misprint for 'ablata' (taken away); rendered 'taken away' as the evident sense (cross-family review pass 2 r01-04).

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Hinc est quod cautissimo divisionis ordine Ecclesia Dei vivi, quae est columna et firmamentum veritatis, tempora venturi Christi venientisque discernit, et omissis sacrificiis quibus Christus passurus promittebatur, hoc sacrificium offert, quo Christus jam passus ostenditur, qui propterea verus est sacerdos, quia semetipsum veram pro nobis hostiam obtulit, sicut Apostolus testatur dicens: «Estote ergo imitatores»[Col. 0021A] «Dei sicut filii charissimi, et ambulate in dilectione, sicut et Christus dilexit nos, et tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis» (I Cor. XI, 1), ut in ipso sacerdote ac sacrificio fieret remissio peccatorum, id est per mediatorum Dei et hominum, hominem Christum Jesum, per quem facta peccatorum purgatione reconciliamur Deo. Non enim nisi peccatis homines separantur a Deo, quorum in hac vita non fit nostra virtute, sed divina miseratione purgatio per indulgentiam illius, non per nostram potentiam, quia et ipsa quantulacunque virtus quae dicitur nostra, illius est nobis bonitate concessa.
chunks.english: This is why the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth, makes such a careful distinction between the times: the time when Christ was still to come, and the time after he has come. The Church sets aside the sacrifices by which Christ’s future suffering was promised, and now offers this sacrifice, by which Christ is shown as already having suffered. He is the true priest precisely because he offered himself for us as the true victim. As the Apostle testifies: “Be imitators of God, then, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us, an offering and a victim to God, a sweet-smelling fragrance”—Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse one. So the forgiveness of sins takes place in this one who is both priest and sacrifice: that is, through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. Through him, once our sins have been cleansed, we are reconciled to God. For nothing separates human beings from God except sins. And in this life, sins are not cleansed by our own strength, but by divine mercy; not through our power, but through God’s forgiveness. Even the little strength that we call our own has been granted to us by his goodness.
chunks.notes: The printed citation is “I Cor. XI, 1,” but the quotation is from Paul's letter to the Ephesians, chapter five, verses one through two. Following rule D026, the English speaks the printed citation and notes the discrepancy. The printed Latin has “per mediatorum Dei et hominum”; translated according to the evident sense as “through the mediator between God and human beings,” corresponding to “per mediatorem.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 5. Propterea ergo nobis per Mediatorem praestita est gratia, ut polluti carne peccati, carnis peccati [Col. 0021B] similitudine mundaremur, per hoc scilicet quod eramus et non eramus. Eramus enim homines, sed justi non eramus; in illius autem incarnatione, natura humana erat, sed justa, non peccatrix erat. Haec est mediatio, qua manus lapsis jacentibusque porrecta est. Hoc est semen dispositum per angelos, in quorum edictis et lux dabatur, quia et unus Deus coli jubebatur, et hic mediator venturus promittebatur. Usus sacramenti fide etiam justi antiqui mundari pie vivendo meruerunt, sicut beatus Petrus apostolus ad quosdam qui in lege justificari quaerebant, manifeste testatur, dicens: «Quid tentatis Dominum, imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque nos, neque patres nostri portare potuimus; sed per fidem Domini Jesu credimus salvari, quemadmodum»[Col. 0021C] «et illi?» (Act. XV, 10.)
chunks.english: For this reason, grace has been given to us through the Mediator: we were defiled by sinful flesh, and we were to be made clean through the likeness of sinful flesh. That is, through what we were and what we were not. We were human beings, but we were not righteous. In his incarnation, there was true human nature, but it was righteous human nature, not sinful. This is the mediation by which a hand was stretched out to those who had fallen and were lying helpless. This is the seed arranged through angels. In their decrees, light was also being given, because they commanded that the one God be worshiped, and they promised that this Mediator would come. By using this sacrament in faith, even the righteous people of old deserved to be cleansed by living devoutly. The blessed apostle Peter bears clear witness to this when he speaks to those who were trying to be justified by the law: “Why are you testing the Lord by placing a yoke on the necks of the disciples, a yoke that neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? Rather, through the faith of the Lord Jesus, we believe that we are saved, in the same way as they are”—the Acts of the Apostles, chapter fifteen, verse ten.
chunks.notes: The citation is printed as Acts of the Apostles, chapter fifteen, verse ten, though the quotation also includes material from verse eleven. The English speaks the printed citation and notes the expanded quotation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Omnis itaque hominum multitudo, propter quos a daemonum dominatione liberandos Christus advenit, in illo habent misericordissimam purgationem et mentis et spiritus et corporis sui. Propterea quippe totum hominem sine peccato ille suscepit, ut totum quo constat homo, a peccatorum peste sanaret. Gratia quippe Dei non potuit gratius commendari, quam ut ipse unicus Dei Filius in se incommutabiliter manens, induceret hominem, et spem dilectionis suae donaret hominibus homine medio, qua ad illum ab hominibus uniretur, qui tam longe erat, immortalis a mortalibus, incommutabilis a commutabilibus, justus ab impiis, beatus a miseris, et quia naturaliter indidit nobis ut beati immortalesque esse cupiamus, manens [Col. 0021D] beatus suscipiensque mortalem, ut nobis tribueret quod amamus, perpetiendo docuit contemnere quod timemus. Hac Dei gratia qua in nos ostendit magnam misericordiam suam, et in hac vita per fidem regimur, et post hanc vitam per ipsam speciem, incommutabilis veritatis ad perfectionem plenissimam perducimur.
chunks.english: So the whole multitude of human beings, for whose sake Christ came to free them from the rule of demons, have in him a most merciful cleansing of mind, spirit, and body. He took up the whole human person without sin, so that everything that makes up a human being might be healed from the plague of sins. God’s grace could not have been presented to us in a more gracious way than this: the only Son of God, while remaining unchangeably himself, took on humanity, and through the human Mediator gave human beings hope in his love. By that love, human beings would be united to the one who had been so far from them: the immortal from mortals, the unchangeable from changeable creatures, the righteous from the ungodly, the blessed from the miserable. And because he has planted in us by nature the desire to be blessed and immortal, he remained blessed while taking on mortality. In order to give us what we love, he taught us, by suffering, to look down on what we fear. By this grace of God, through which he has shown us his great mercy, we are guided in this life by faith; and after this life, by the direct vision of unchangeable truth, we are brought to the fullest perfection.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 6. Hanc igitur gratiam purgationis et redemptionis nostrae, quam nobis Dominus et Salvator in sacramento sui corporis et sanguinis commendavit, longe antequam pateretur in populis praedicavit; sed pridie quam pateretur, id est ea nocte qua tradebatur, in coena discipulis suis tradidit. Nam beatus Joannes evangelista statim post illud de quinque panibus miraculum, [Col. 0022A] quo in quinque millia hominum satiata sunt, narrat eum fugisse in montem, declinando scilicet a turbis, quae tanti signi admiratione permotae, cupiebant rapere et facere eum regem, et mox veniente nocte ambulantem super mare venisse Capharnaum, atque ibi jam die altera occurrentibus sibi turbis et inter alia quaerentibus et dicentibus: «Quid faciemus ut operemur opera Dei?» respondisse eis: «Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum quem misit ille.» Cumque respondissent: «Quod ergo tu signum facis, ut videamus et credamus tibi? quid operaris? Patres nostri manna manducaverunt in deserto, sicut scriptum est: Panem de coelo dedit eis manducare. Dixit eis Jesus: Amen, amen dico vobis, non Moyses dedit vobis panem de coelo, sed Pater meus dat vobis»[Col. 0022B] «panem de coelo verum. Panis enim Dei est, qui descondit de coelo, et dat vitam mundo.» Et post paululum: «Ego sum panis vitae, qui venit ad me non esuriet, et qui credit in me non sitiet unquam.» Et iterum: «Amen, amen dico vobis, qui credit in me habet vitam aeternam. Ego sum panis vitae: patres vestri manducaverunt manna in deserto et mortui sunt. Hic est panis de coelo descendens, ut si quis ex ipso manducaverit, non moriatur. Ego sum panis vivus qui de coelo descendi: si quis manducaverit ex hoc pane, vivet in aeternum. Et panis quem ego dabo, caro mea est pro mundi vita.» Et rursus post aliqua: «Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis; qui manducat meam carnem, et bibit meum sanguinem, habet vitam aeternam, et»[Col. 0022C] «ego resuscitabo eum in novissimo die. Caro enim mea vere est cibus et sanguis meus vere est potus: qui manducat meam carnem et bibit meum sanguinem, in me manet et ego in illo. Sicut misit me vivens Pater et ego vivo propter Patrem, et qui manducat me, et ipse vivet propter me.» Post hoc subjunxit Evangelista: «Haec dixit in synogoga docens in Capharnaum» (Joan. VI, 28, 35, 47, 54, 59), quod totum, sicut ipse Evangelii secundum Joannem textus ostendit, manifeste anno integro ante passionem Domini gestum est. Nam sicut idem evangelista scribit, quando illud de quinque panibus miraculum factum est, «Proximum erat pascha, dies festus Judaeorum» (Ibid., vers. 4); nec tamen in ipso, sed in pascha anni sequentis eum ad passionem venisse commemorat.
chunks.english: This grace of our cleansing and redemption was entrusted to us by the Lord and Savior in the sacrament of his body and blood. Long before he suffered, he proclaimed it publicly among the people; but on the day before he suffered, that is, on the night when he was handed over, he handed it on to his disciples at supper. Blessed John the Evangelist says that immediately after the miracle of the five loaves, by which five thousand people were fed, Jesus fled to the mountain. He withdrew from the crowds, because they were stirred by admiration for so great a sign and wanted to seize him and make him king. Then, when night came, he walked on the sea and came to Capernaum. The next day, when the crowds met him there, they asked, among other things, “What must we do to perform the works of God?” He answered them, “This is the work of God: that you believe in the one whom he has sent.” They replied, “Then what sign do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What work do you do? Our fathers ate manna in the desert, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat.” Jesus said to them, “Amen, amen, I tell you: Moses did not give you the bread from heaven. Rather, my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” A little later he says, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.” And again: “Amen, amen, I tell you: whoever believes in me has eternal life. I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the desert and died. This is the bread coming down from heaven, so that if anyone eats from it, he will not die. I am the living bread who came down from heaven. If anyone eats from this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, for the life of the world.” And again, after some further words: “Amen, amen, I tell you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so also the one who eats me will live because of me.” After this the Evangelist adds, “He said these things while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum”—the Gospel of John, chapter six, verses twenty-eight, thirty-five, forty-seven, fifty-four, and fifty-nine. As the very text of the Gospel according to John shows, all of this clearly took place a full year before the Lord’s passion. For, as the same Evangelist writes, when the miracle of the five loaves took place, “the Passover, the feast day of the Jews, was near”—the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse four. Yet John records that Jesus came to his passion not at that Passover, but at the Passover of the following year.
chunks.notes: The printed citation lists selected verses in John chapter six: twenty-eight, thirty-five, forty-seven, fifty-four, and fifty-nine. The quotation actually draws from a broader sequence in John chapter six. “Ibid., vers. 4” has been made explicit as the Gospel of John, chapter six, verse four.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Hinc est quod [Col. 0022D] in illa coena paschali, quando Dominus traditus est, nihil de ipso corporis et sanguinis ejus mysterio idem beatus Joannes commemorat; quia videlicet copiosius hoc et sublimius in praecedentibus Evangelii sui partibus explicaverat, et a reliquis tribus evangelistis, quod in eadem coena in commemoratione Dominicae passionis ad salutem fidelium fuerat traditum, diligenter noverat commendatum. Verba quippe Matthaei haec sunt: «Coenantibus autem eis, accepit Jesus panem, et benedixit, et fregit, deditque discipulis suis et ait: Accipite et comedite: hoc est corpus meum. Et accipiens calicem gratias egit, et dedit illis, dicens: Bibite ex hoc omnes. Hic est enim sanguis meus Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effundetur in»[Col. 0023A] «remissionem peccatorum» (Matth. XXVI, 26). Marcus vero sic ait: «Et manducantibus illis, accepit Jesus panem, et benedicens fregit, et dedit eis, et ait: Sumite: Hoc est corpus meum. Et accepto calice, gratias agens dedit eis. Et biberunt ex illo omnes, et ait illis: Hic est sanguis meus Novi Testamenti, qui pro multis effunditur» (Marc. XIV, 22). Lucae vero his verbis narratio explicatur: «Et accepto calice gratias egit, et dixit, Accipite et dividite inter vos. Dico enim vobis quod non bibam de generatione vitis, donec regnum Dei veniat. Et accepto pane, gratias egit, et fregit, et dedit eis dicens: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis datur. Hoc facite in meam commemorationem. Similiter et calicem, postquam coenavit dicens: Hic calix Novum Testamentum est in sanguine meo, qui»[Col. 0023B] «pro vobis funditur» (Luc. XXII, 17).
chunks.english: This is why, at that paschal supper when the Lord was handed over, blessed John says nothing about the mystery of Christ’s body and blood itself. Clearly, he had already explained it more fully and more sublimely in the earlier parts of his Gospel. He also knew that the other three Evangelists had carefully handed on what was given at that same supper, in remembrance of the Lord’s passion, for the salvation of the faithful. Matthew’s words are these: “While they were at supper, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said, ‘Take and eat. This is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying, ‘Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’”—the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-six, verse twenty-six. Mark says it this way: “While they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessing it, broke it, gave it to them, and said, ‘Take. This is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them. And they all drank from it. And he said to them, ‘This is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many’”—the Gospel of Mark, chapter fourteen, verse twenty-two. Luke’s account is given in these words: “And taking the cup, he gave thanks and said, ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that I will not drink from the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.’ And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, ‘This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying, ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which is poured out for you’”—the Gospel of Luke, chapter twenty-two, verse seventeen.
chunks.notes: The printed citations give Matthew chapter twenty-six, verse twenty-six; Mark chapter fourteen, verse twenty-two; and Luke chapter twenty-two, verse seventeen, though each quotation extends beyond the single printed verse. The English speaks the printed citations as required. The printed Latin has “de generatione vitis”; translated according to the evident biblical sense as “from the fruit of the vine,” where the expected reading would be “de genimine vitis.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Beatus etiam Paulus, commemorans sacratissimae illius coenae mysterium, inter alia sic dicit: «Ego enim accepi a Domino, quod et tradidi vobis, quoniam Dominus Jesus, in qua nocte tradebatur, accepit panem, et gratias agens fregit et dixit: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis tradetur; hoc facite in meam commemorationem. Similiter et calicem postquam caenavit dicens: Hic calix Novum Testamentum est in meo sanguine. Hoc facite quotiescunque bibetis in meam commemorationem» (I Cor. XI, 25). Quantum est istud et ineffabile salutis mysterium et pietatis sacramentum, tanta contestatione praedictum, tanta veritate commendatum, ut prius hoc Dominus corpus et sanguinem suum assereret, quam pro nobis suum corpus [Col. 0023C] et sanguinem traderetur nemo enim potest passionis Domini corporisque ejus et sanguinis pro majestate rei sacramenta cognoscere.
chunks.english: Blessed Paul also, recalling the mystery of that most holy supper, says among other things: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was being handed over, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said, ‘This is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying, ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me’”—Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse twenty-five. How great this mystery of salvation is! How beyond words is this sacrament of loving devotion! It was foretold with such solemn witness and entrusted with such truth that the Lord declared it to be his body and blood before his body and blood were handed over for us. No one can grasp the sacraments of the Lord’s passion, and of his body and blood, in a way that matches the majesty of the reality itself.
chunks.notes: The printed citation is Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse twenty-five, though the quotation begins earlier in verses twenty-three and twenty-four and continues through verse twenty-five. The Latin punctuation around “traderetur nemo enim” is syntactically compressed; translated as two sentences for clarity.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 7. (FULG. epist. 14, ad Ferrandum, n. 43.) Notandum quoque diligenter, quod in eadem coena et Judaicum Dominus pascha comedit, quod oportebat auferri, et sacramentum corporis sui et sanguinis dedit, quod ad salutem fidelium oportebat institui. «Desiderio,» inquit, «desideravi hoc pascha manducare vobiscum antequam patiar.» Manducavit ergo pascha, quo passurus significabatur, antequam pro nobis voluntarie pateretur. Comedit pascha Judaeorum, quo promissus est Christus, ut veniret ad pascha nostrum, quod immolatus est Christus.
chunks.english: [Fulgentius] We must also note carefully that, at this same supper, the Lord both ate the Jewish Passover, which had to be taken away, and gave the sacrament of his body and blood, which had to be established for the salvation of the faithful. He says, “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” So he ate the Passover by which his coming suffering was signified, before he voluntarily suffered for us. He ate the Passover of the Jews, in which Christ was promised, so that he might come to our Passover, in which Christ was sacrificed.
chunks.notes: Printed marginal source siglum: “FULG. epist. 14, ad Ferrandum, n. 43.” Rendered according to the work-specific rule as “[Fulgentius].” The quotation “With desire I have desired…” is from the Gospel of Luke, chapter twenty-two, verse fifteen, but no scripture citation is printed here.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 8. (AUG., epist. 54, ad Januarium.) Aperte enim [Col. 0023D] dicit Evangelium, quod manducantibus illis accepit Jesus panem et benedixit. Cum etiam superius dixisset: Cum sero autem factum esset, discumbebat cum duodecim. Et manducantibus illis dixit: Unus ex vobis tradet me, post enim tradidit sacramentum; unde liquido apparet, quando primo acceperunt discipuli corpus et sanguinem Domini, non eos accepisse jejunos, nequaquam tamen propterea calumniandum est universae Ecclesiae, quod a jejunis semper accipitur. Ex hoc enim placuit Spiritui sancto, ut in honorem tanti sacramenti in os Christiani prius Dominicum corpus [Col. 0024A] intraret, quam ceteri cibi. Nam ideo per universum orbem mos iste servatur, neque enim quia post cibos dedit Dominus, propterea pransi aut coenati fratres ad illud sacramentum accipiendum convenire debebunt, aut sicut faciebant quos Apostolus arguit et emendat, mensis suis ista miscere; ait enim: «Convenientibus vobis in unum, jam non est Dominicam caenam manducare» (I Cor. XI, 18), hanc ipsam acceptionem eucharistiae Dominicam coenam vocans. «Unusquisque enim,» inquit, «suam caenam praeoccupat ad manducandum» (Ibid., vers. 21); unde et indigne dicit acceptum ab eis, qui non discernebant a caeteris cibis veneratione singulariter debita. Continuo quippe cum dixisset «judicium sibi manducat et bibit,» subjecit, «non dijudicans corpus Domini» (Ibid., vers. 29); [Col. 0024B] namque Salvator quo vehementius commendaret mysterii illius altitudinem, ultimum hoc voluit infigere cordibus et memoriae discipulorum, a quibus ad passionem digressurus erat; et ideo non praecipit, quo deinceps ordine sumeretur, ut apostolis, per quos ordinare Ecclesias disposuerat servaret hunc locum.
chunks.english: [Augustine] For the Gospel says plainly that, while they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it. Earlier it had also said, “When evening came, he was reclining at table with the twelve. And while they were eating, he said, ‘One of you will betray me.’” After that, he handed on the sacrament. So it is completely clear that, when the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord, they did not receive it fasting. Still, no one should use that fact to criticize the universal Church, because the sacrament is always received by people who are fasting. For from that time on the Holy Spirit was pleased that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the mouth of a Christian before any other food. That is why this custom is observed throughout the whole world. And because the Lord gave it after food, that does not mean that brothers and sisters should come to receive this sacrament after lunch or dinner, or mix it with their own meals, as those people did whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects. For he says, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse eighteen, “When you come together as one, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper,” calling this very receiving of the Eucharist the Lord’s supper. And he says, in the same chapter, verse twenty-one, “Each one goes ahead with his own supper to eat.” For this reason he says that it was received unworthily by those who did not distinguish it from other foods with the special reverence owed to it. Indeed, immediately after saying, “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself,” he added, in the same chapter, verse twenty-nine, “not discerning the body of the Lord.” The Savior, then, wanted to commend the depth of that mystery all the more powerfully. Since he was about to leave his disciples and go to his Passion, he chose to impress this last thing on their hearts and memory. And therefore he did not command in what order it should afterward be received, so that he might leave this matter to the apostles, through whom he had determined to order the Churches.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “AUG., epist. 54, ad Januarium.” The first Gospel quotation is from the passion narrative; the printed text gives no citation. The printed citation “I Cor. XI, 18” is spoken as printed, though the quoted wording corresponds more closely to Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse twenty. “Ibid.” has been expanded in English as “in the same chapter.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 9. (CYPRIAN., epist. 63, ad Cecil.) Neque enim quia post coenam calicem obtulit Dominus, etiam Dominici diei sacrificium post coenam celebrare debemus. Christum offerre oportebat circa vesperam diei, ut hora ipsa sacrificii ostenderet occasum et vesperam mundi, sicut de paschali agno in Exodo scriptum est: «Et immolabit eum omnis multitudo filiorum Israel ad vesperam» (Exod. XII, 6). Et iterum in psalmis: «Allevatio manuum mearum sacrificium vespertinum» [Col. 0024C] (Psal. CXL, 2).
chunks.english: [Cyprian] For although the Lord offered the cup after supper, that does not mean we too must celebrate the sacrifice of the Lord’s Day after supper. Christ had to make the offering toward the evening of the day, so that the very hour of the sacrifice would point to the decline and evening of the world. As it is written about the Passover lamb in Exodus, chapter twelve, verse six: “The whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening.” And again in the Psalms, Psalm one hundred forty, verse two: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “CYPRIAN., epist. 63, ad Cecil.” The Psalm citation is rendered as printed. In many modern English Bibles this is Psalm one hundred forty-one, verse two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 10. (AUG., epist. 149, ad Paulinum, n. 16.) Nos autem resurrectionem Domini mane celebramus. Cum vero ait Apostolus de hoc sacramento loquens: «Propter quod, fratres, cum convenitis ad manducandum, invicem exspectate. Si quis esurit, domi manducet, ut non in judicium conveniatis,» statim subtexuit, «caetera autem cum venero ordinabo» (I Cor. XI, 33). Unde intelligi datur quia multum erat ut in Epistola totum illis agendi ordinem insinuaret, quem universa per orbem servat Ecclesia, ab ipso ordinatum esse, quod nulla horum diversitate variatur. Nam et ubi ad Timotheum scribens ait: «Obsecro itaque primo omnium fieri obsecrationes, orationes, interpellationes, gratiarum actiones» (I Tim. II, 1), hoc constituisse intelligitur, [Col. 0024D] quod omnis et pene omnis frequentat Ecclesia, ut obsecrationes accipiamus dictas quae fiunt in celebratione sacramentorum, antequam illud quod est in Domini mensa incipiat benedici; orationes, cum benedicitur et sanctificatur, et ad distribuendum comminuitur, quam totam benedictionem fere omnis Ecclesia Dominica oratione concludit. Interpellationes autem, sive, ut quidam codices habent, postulationes fiunt, cum populus benedicitur. Tunc enim antistites velut advocati, susceptos suos per manus impositionem misericordissimae offerunt potestati. [Col. 0025A] Quibus peractis, et participato tanto sacramento, gratiarum actio cuncta concludit, quam in his etiam verbis ultimam commendavit Apostolus.
chunks.english: [Augustine] But we celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning. When the Apostle, speaking about this sacrament, says, “Therefore, brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment,” he immediately adds, “The rest I will set in order when I come,” in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse thirty-three. From this we are given to understand that it would have been too much for him to explain to them in a letter the entire order of the action. This order, which the whole Church throughout the world observes, is to be understood as arranged by the Apostle himself, in so far as it is not varied by any of these differences. So too, when writing to Timothy, he says, in Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse one: “I urge, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made.” He is understood to have established what every Church, or almost every Church, regularly does. We should understand “supplications” as those made in the celebration of the sacraments before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed. “Prayers” are made when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution; nearly the whole Church concludes this whole blessing with the Lord’s Prayer. “Intercessions,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “petitions,” are made when the people are blessed. For then the bishops, like advocates, offer those entrusted to them, through the laying on of hands, to the most merciful power of God. When these things have been completed, and when so great a sacrament has been shared, thanksgiving brings everything to its close; and the Apostle commended thanksgiving as the last of these in the very words just quoted.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “AUG., epist. 149, ad Paulinum, n. 16.” The citation “I Cor. XI, 33” is spoken as printed, though the quoted passage includes material from Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verses thirty-three through thirty-four. “Actio” is rendered as “the action,” referring to the eucharistic canon or ordered liturgical rite.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Haec autem causa praecipua fuit ista dicendi, ut his breviter praescriptis atque significatis, non putaretur negligendum esse quod sequitur, «pro omnibus hominibus, pro regibus et his qui in sublimitate sunt, ut quietam et tranquillam vitam agamus in omni pietate et castitate» (I Tim. II, 2), ne quisquam, sicut se habet humanae cogitationis infirmitas, aestimaret non esse ista facienda pro iis a quibus persecutionem patiebatur Ecclesia, cum membra Christi ex omni essent hominum genere colligenda. Unde adjungit et dicit: «Hoc enim bonum est et acceptum coram Salvatore nostro Domino, qui omnes homines vult salvos fieri, et in»[Col. 0025B] «agnitionem veritatis venire» (Ibid., vers. 3). Et ne quisquam diceret posse esse salutis viam in bona conversatione et unius Dei omnipotentis cultu, sive participatione corporis et sanguinis Christi: «Unus enim Deus,» inquit, «unus enim Mediator Dei et hominum homo Jesus Christus,» ut illud quod dixerat, «omnes homines vult salvos fieri,» nullo alio modo intelligatur praestari, nisi per mediatorem, non Deum, quod semper erat Verbum, sed hominem Christum Jesum cum «Verbum caro factum est et habitavit in nobis.» Ideo enim Christus mediator Dei et hominum dictus est inter Deum immortalem et mortalem hominem Deus et homo reconcilians hominem Deo, verus rex, verus sacerdos. Ne ergo peccet homo, a rege Christo regatur; si forte peccaverit, ab eodem sacerdote Christo expietur.
chunks.english: The main reason he said these things was this: after briefly prescribing and indicating this liturgical order, he did not want what follows to be neglected.
