He continues, in Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse two, “for all people, for kings and for those in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness and chastity.” Otherwise, because human thinking is weak, someone might suppose that these prayers should not be made for those from whom the Church was suffering persecution. But the members of Christ were to be gathered from every class of humanity. Therefore he adds and says, in the same chapter, verse three, “For this is good and acceptable before our Savior the Lord, who wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” And to keep anyone from saying that there could be a way of salvation through good conduct and the worship of the one almighty God, apart from participation in the body and blood of Christ, he says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ.” In this way, the statement that God “wants all people to be saved” must be understood as being fulfilled in no other way than through the mediator: not through Christ as God, which the Word always was, but through the man Christ Jesus, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” For Christ is called the mediator between God and human beings because, as God and man, he stands between the immortal God and mortal humanity, reconciling humanity to God. He is the true king and the true priest. Therefore, so that a human being may not sin, let that person be ruled by Christ the king; and if that person should sin, let that person be cleansed by the same Christ, the priest.
chunks.notes: “Ibid.” has been expanded as “in the same chapter.” The printed reference “Ibid., vers. 3” is spoken as printed, though the quotation includes wording that extends into Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse four. The sentence “apart from participation in the body and blood of Christ” translates the Latin “sive participatione corporis et sanguinis Christi”; the argument requires the sense that salvation is not to be separated from Christ’s mediation and sacramental participation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0025C] 11. Primo igitur convenientibus in unum, et astantibus in domo Dei fidelibus, praecedente modulatione divinarum laudum, praecedente lectione apostolorum et Evangeliorum, praecedente etiam nonnunquam sermone et allocutione magistrorum, subjuncta quoque symboli confessione, et oblatione populorum, et initiata consecratione sacramentorum, in quibus omnibus mens astantium ad divina et coelestia cogitanda ac desideranda praeparatur, assistit sacerdos altari, et celebraturus divina mysteria, Ecclesiam salutando orat, et orando salutat dicens:
chunks.english: So, first, the faithful come together and stand in the house of God. The singing of divine praise has gone before; the reading from the apostles and the Gospels has gone before; sometimes a sermon and exhortation by the teachers has also gone before. The confession of the Creed has been added, the people’s offering has been made, and the consecration of the sacraments has begun. Through all these things, the minds of those standing there are prepared to think about and desire divine and heavenly realities. Then the priest stands at the altar, about to celebrate the divine mysteries. He prays as he greets the Church, and greets it as he prays, saying:

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 12. «Dominus vobiscum.» Qui salutationis sermo non humano arbitrio compositus, sed ex divinae Scripturae auctoritate desumptus probatur, ubi frequenter et singulariter et pluraliter positus legitur. [Col. 0025D] Singulariter, sicut ait angelus ad beatam Mariam: «Ave gratia plena, Dominus tecum» (Luc. I, 28); et sicut ad Gedeon similiter salutando dixit: «Dominus tecum, virorum fortissime» (Jud. VI, 12). Pluraliter autem, sicut in libro Ruth, qui utique sicut caeteri sacrae Scripturae libri divina et mystica continet, legitur Booz salutando dixisse messoribus: «Dominus vobiscum.» Cui et ipsi resalutantes dixerunt: «Benedicat tibi Dominus» (Ruth. II, 4). Et sicut in historia libri Paralipomenon propheta missus a Deo invenitur salutasse Asa regem Juda cum exercitu suo, invocato Dei auxilio, victores de praelio revertentes. Ait enim: «Dominus vobiscum, quia»[Col. 0026A] «fuistis cum eo.» Et addidit: «Si quaesieritis eum, invenietis: si autem dereliqueritis illum, derelinquet vos» (I Par. XXVIII, 9).
chunks.english: “The Lord be with you.” This greeting is shown not to have been composed by human choice, but to have been taken from the authority of divine Scripture, where it is often found in both the singular and the plural. In the singular, the angel says to blessed Mary, in the Gospel of Luke, chapter one, verse twenty-eight: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” Likewise, in greeting Gideon, the angel said, in Judges, chapter six, verse twelve: “The Lord is with you, most valiant of men.” In the plural, we read in the book of Ruth, which, like the other books of sacred Scripture, certainly contains divine and mystical meaning, that Boaz greeted the reapers by saying, “The Lord be with you.” And they, greeting him in return, said, “May the Lord bless you,” in Ruth, chapter two, verse four. So also, in the narrative of the book of Chronicles, a prophet sent by God is found to have greeted Asa, king of Judah, together with his army, as they were returning victorious from battle after calling on God’s help. For he says: “The Lord is with you, because you have been with him.” And he added: “If you seek him, you will find him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you,” in First Chronicles, chapter twenty-eight, verse nine.
chunks.notes: The printed citation “I Par. XXVIII, 9” is rendered in English as “First Chronicles, chapter twenty-eight, verse nine,” according to the printed reference. The quotation actually corresponds to Second Chronicles, chapter fifteen, verse two, not First Chronicles, chapter twenty-eight, verse nine.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Unde patet quia sicut NIHIL PEJUS potest esse homini quam derelinquere Deum et derelinqui a Deo: ita econtrario nihil melius est quam habere Deum et esse cum Deo. Et quia salutare nihil est aliud quam salutem optare, haec est vera salutatio, verae salutis optatio, id est cum ecclesia sua tanquam in templo suo, cum dicit Apostolus: «Templum enim Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos» (I Cor. III, 16). Et Ecclesia habet Dominum secum inhabitantem et illuminantem, regentem et protegentem, ut ille sit ei Deus, et illa sit populus, sicut propheta promisit dicens: «Et inhabitabo et inambulabo cum illis, et ero eis Deus, et erunt ipsi populus» (II [Col. 0026B] Cor. VI, 16), ut dum tantae beatitudinis dono Ecclesia Dei et possidet Dominum et possidetur a Deo, quatenus et ipsa sit haereditas Domini, et Dominus pars haereditatis ejus, impleatur in illa quod Psalmista ait: «Beata gens, cujus Dominus Deus ejus, populus quem elegit in haereditatem sibi» (Psal. XXXII, 12).
chunks.english: From this it is clear that, just as nothing can be worse for a person than to abandon God and be abandoned by God, so, on the other hand, nothing is better than to have God and to be with God. And because to greet someone is nothing other than to wish that person salvation and well-being, this is the true greeting: the wish for true salvation. It means that the Lord is with his Church as in his temple, as the Apostle says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter three, verse sixteen: “For the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.” And the Church has the Lord with it: dwelling in it and enlightening it, ruling it and protecting it, so that he may be its God and it may be his people. As the prophet promised when he said, in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verse sixteen: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” Thus, by the gift of such blessedness, the Church of God both possesses the Lord and is possessed by God, so that the Church is the Lord’s inheritance and the Lord is the Church’s share of inheritance. In the Church, then, what the Psalmist says is fulfilled, in Psalm thirty-two, verse twelve: “Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God, the people whom he chose as an inheritance for himself.”
chunks.notes: The citation “II Cor. VI, 16” is spoken as printed. Paul is quoting and combining Old Testament covenant promises. The Psalm citation is rendered as printed; in many modern English Bibles this is Psalm thirty-three, verse twelve.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Hoc est enim summum hominis bonum possidere Deum, et possideri a Deo; ipsum solum diligere et ipsi soli servire, illi soli adhaerere, ut dicat illi anima devota: «Mihi autem adhaerere Deo bonum» (Psal. LXXII, 28). Et iterum: «Adhaesit anima mea post te» (Psal. LXII, 9), ut adhaerens Domino, unus cum eo spiritus fiat, dicente Apostolo: «Qui adhaeret Domino, unus spiritus est» (I Cor. VI, 17). Nam et ipse Apostolus in Epistolis suis ita salutat dicens, ut [Col. 0026C] aliquando dicat: «Dominus cum omnibus vobis;» aliquando: «Deus autem pacis sit cum omnibus vobis:» item aliquando: «Gratia Domini nostri Jesus Christi sit cum spiritu vestro, fratres, amen» (Gal. VI, 18). Et nonnunquam sub distinctione personarum, totam invocans Trinitatem, ita salutat: «Gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi et charitas Dei, et communicatio sancti Spiritus sit cum omnibus vobis» (II Cor. XIII, 13). In quibus omnibus hoc optat fidelibus scribens, quod sacerdos ad altare assistens, scilicet ut habentes Deum non deserantur ab eo. Recte ergo Ecclesia tam salubri sacerdotis voce accepta, et ipsa resalutando orat, et orando resalutat sacerdotem, dicens:
chunks.english: For this is the highest good of a human being: to possess God and to be possessed by God; to love him alone, to serve him alone, and to cling to him alone, so that the devout soul may say to him, in Psalm seventy-two, verse twenty-eight: “For me, it is good to cling to God.” And again, in Psalm sixty-two, verse nine: “My soul has clung after you.” In this way, by clinging to the Lord, the soul becomes one spirit with him, as the Apostle says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verse seventeen: “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.” The Apostle himself also gives this kind of greeting in his letters. Sometimes he says, “The Lord be with all of you.” Sometimes, “May the God of peace be with all of you.” Again, he says, in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter six, verse eighteen: “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.” And sometimes, distinguishing the persons and invoking the whole Trinity, he greets them in this way, in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter thirteen, verse thirteen: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.” In all these greetings, as he writes to the faithful, he desires the same thing that the priest desires as he stands at the altar: that those who have God may not be abandoned by him. Therefore, when the Church receives such a saving word from the priest, it rightly prays as it greets him in return, and greets him in return as it prays, saying:
chunks.notes: Psalm citations are rendered as printed; in many modern English Bibles Psalm seventy-two is Psalm seventy-three, and Psalm sixty-two is Psalm sixty-three. The citation “II Cor. XIII, 13” is spoken as printed; in many modern verse numberings this is Second Corinthians, chapter thirteen, verse fourteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 13. «Et cum Spiritu tuo.» Nihil enim melius invenit [Col. 0026D] Ecclesia quod optaret sacerdoti, nisi quod sacerdos optat Ecclesiae, id est ut idem Dominus qui dignatur esse cum Ecclesia, dignetur etiam esse cum spiritu sacerdotis, ac sic in utroque benigna illa Domini promissio impleatur, qua ascensurus in coelum omnibus fidelibus promisit dicens: «Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem saeculi» (Matth. XXVIII, 20). Hoc ergo tantum bonum sibi invicem optant et postulant, et sacerdos Ecclesiae, et Ecclesia sacerdoti, ut sicut ejus gratia illuminatur, ejus praesentia confortatur, ejus protectione munitur; semper eum manere nobiscum, quemadmodum est pollicitus, sentiamus. Hoc etiam modo [Col. 0027A] aliquoties salutat Apostolus, et pluraliter, ut superius memoravimus, ubi ait: «Dominus Jesus Christus cum spiritu vestro, fratres, amen» (Gal. VI, 18). Et singulariter, ubi ad Timotheum salutans dicit: «Dominus Jesus Christus cum spiritu tuo, amen.» Et bene Dominus cum spiritu hominis esse optatur, quia in spiritu et mente rationali creatus est homo ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei: et ibi est capax divinae gratiae et illuminationis, ut in quantum ei datur possit sentire dulcedinem suavitatis, et splendorem praesentiae ejus, ut fiat in eo illud quod Psalmista ait: «Gustate et videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus» (Psal. XXXIII, 9). Et iterum: «Accedite ad cum, et illuminamini, et vultus vestri non erubescent» (Ibid., vers. 6). Sic namque sanctificato spiritu hominis [Col. 0027B] per inhabitationem Dei, efficitur homo etiam in corpore templum. Unde ait apostolus: «Corpora vestra templum est Spiritus sancti quem habetis a Deo» (I Cor. VI, 19).
chunks.english:
“And with your spirit.” The Church can find nothing better to wish for the priest than what the priest wishes for the Church: that the same Lord who is pleased to be with the Church may also be pleased to be with the spirit of the priest. In this way, for both of them, that gracious promise of the Lord is fulfilled—the promise he made to all the faithful when he was about to ascend into heaven: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-eight, verse twenty.

So this is the great blessing that priest and Church ask and wish for one another: that, enlightened by his grace, strengthened by his presence, and guarded by his protection, we may experience him remaining with us always, just as he promised.

The Apostle also uses this kind of greeting at times. He uses it in the plural, as mentioned earlier, when he says, “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen,” in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter six, verse eighteen. And he uses it in the singular when, greeting Timothy, he says, “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

It is fitting to wish that the Lord be with the human spirit, because the human being was created in spirit and rational mind according to the image and likeness of God. There, in the spirit and mind, the human person is able to receive divine grace and illumination, so that, as far as it is granted, one can perceive the sweetness of his goodness and the brightness of his presence. Then what the Psalmist says comes true within that person: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet,” in Psalm thirty-three, verse nine. And again: “Come to him, and be enlightened, and your faces will not be ashamed,” in Psalm thirty-three, verse six.

For when the human spirit has been made holy by God dwelling within it, then the person becomes a temple even in the body. Hence the Apostle says, “Your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God,” in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verse nineteen.
chunks.notes: The printed citation to Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter six, verse eighteen is rendered as printed; the Vulgate form begins, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ...” The singular greeting to Timothy is not given a printed biblical citation here; it corresponds closely to Paul’s second letter to Timothy, chapter four, verse twenty-two. In the Psalm quotation, the printed Latin reads “ad cum,” but the sense requires “ad eum,” “to him”; translated accordingly. The quotation from Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians has the printed plural “Corpora vestra,” “your bodies,” with singular “templum est,” “is the temple”; the biblical text more commonly has the singular “your body.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Sed et illa salutatio episcopalis ad populum, qua dicitur «Pax vobiscum,» sive «Pax vobis,» similiter non humano sensu inventa, sed de Scripturae sanctae auctoritate sumpta est. Nam et in Veteri Testamento invenitur dixisse angelus Danieli prophetae: «Noli timere, vir desideriorum, pax tibi, confortare, et esto robustus» (Dan. X, 19). Et in Novo, id est in Evangelio, pene semper ita Dominus legitur apostolos salutasse dicendo: «Pax vobis;» et eisdem apostolis eamdem salutationis formam commendavit dicens: «In quamcunque autem domum intraveritis, salutate eam dicentes: Pax huic domui, et si ibi fuerit»[Col. 0027C] «filius pacis, requiescet pax vestra super illum: sin autem, pax vestra ad vos revertetur» (Matth. X, 13). Merito ergo et apostolorum successores, id est ecclesiarum praesules hac salutatione utuntur, domum Dei salutantes, ubi oportet omnes esse filios pacis: «Beati» enim «pacifici, quoniam ipsi filii Dei vocabuntur» (Matth. V, 9), ut salutatio pacis super eos requiescens, et salutantibus et salutatis possit esse fructuosa. Pax autem quae sive per angelum, sive per Dominum, sive per pastores ecclesiarum fidelibus imprecatur, non est mundana aut caduca, sed divina et aeterna, quae nos Deo conciliat, et contra tentationes diaboli atque adversitates saeculi ipsius protectione munitas, tranquilla proximis charitate conjunget. Hanc enim Dominus Ecclesiae suae commendavit [Col. 0027D] dicens: «Pacem relinquo vobis, pacem meam do vobis.» Et continuo subjunxit, «non quomodo hic mundus dat, ego do vobis» (Joan. XIV, 27). De hac iterum dicit: «Haec locutus sum vobis, ut in me pacem habeatis; in mundo pressuram habebitis, sed confidite, ego vici mundum» (Joan. XVI, 33). Hanc et Apostolus fidelibus implorat dicens: «Et pax Dei quae exsuperat omnem sensum, custodiat corda vestra et intelligentias vestras in Christo Jesu» (Phil. IV, 7). Quae pax si omni tempore servanda est, et ubique fideliter tenenda, quanto attentius et devotius ea hora cum in domo Domini et in conspectu Dei assistitur, et vota et munera omnium sacris altaribus offeruntur; quando aliter divinam majestatem nobis propitiare [Col. 0028A] non possumus, nisi sincero charitatis affectu illud implere studeamus, quod de hac re specialiter Dominus praecipit dicens: «Si offers munus tuum ad altare, et ibi recordatus fueris, quia frater tuus habet aliquid adversum te, relinque ibi munus tuum ante altare, et vade prius reconciliari fratri tuo, et tunc veniens offeres munus tuum» (Matth. V, 23).
chunks.english:
Likewise, the bishop’s greeting to the people—when he says, “Peace be with you,” or, “Peace be to you”—was not invented by human cleverness. It too was taken from the authority of Holy Scripture.

In the Old Testament, the angel is found saying to the prophet Daniel: “Do not fear, man of desires. Peace be to you. Be strengthened, and be strong,” in Daniel, chapter ten, verse nineteen. And in the New Testament, that is, in the Gospel, the Lord is almost always read as greeting the apostles in this way, saying, “Peace be to you.” He also entrusted this same form of greeting to those apostles when he said: “Into whatever house you enter, greet it, saying, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, your peace will return to you,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter ten, verse thirteen.

So it is fitting that the successors of the apostles—that is, the rulers of the churches—use this greeting when they greet the house of God, where everyone ought to be a child of peace. For Scripture says, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter five, verse nine. Then the greeting of peace, resting upon them, can bear fruit both for those who give the greeting and for those who receive it.

But the peace that is invoked upon the faithful—whether by an angel, by the Lord, or by the shepherds of the churches—is not worldly or passing. It is divine and eternal. It reconciles us to God; it guards us, under his protection, against the temptations of the devil and the hardships of this world; and it joins us calmly to our neighbors in love.

This is the peace the Lord entrusted to his Church when he said, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” And immediately he added, “Not as this world gives do I give to you,” in the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, verse twenty-seven. Again he says of this peace: “I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have distress; but take courage: I have conquered the world,” in the Gospel of John, chapter sixteen, verse thirty-three.

The Apostle also asks this peace for the faithful when he says: “And may the peace of God, which surpasses every understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus,” in Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter four, verse seven.

If this peace must be preserved at every time, and faithfully kept everywhere, then how much more carefully and devoutly must it be kept at that hour when we stand in the house of the Lord and in the sight of God, and when the prayers and offerings of all are presented on the holy altars. At that moment, we cannot make the divine Majesty favorable to us in any other way unless, with sincere love, we make every effort to fulfill what the Lord specifically commands about this matter: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and first go be reconciled to your brother; and then come and offer your gift,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter five, verse twenty-three.
chunks.notes: The citation printed as the Gospel of Matthew, chapter ten, verse thirteen is rendered as printed. The wording conflates Matthew chapter ten, verses twelve through thirteen with Luke chapter ten, verses five through six, especially the phrase “son of peace.” The final Gospel quotation is cited as the Gospel of Matthew, chapter five, verse twenty-three, but the quoted material continues into verse twenty-four.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 14. (GREG., homil. 8 in Ezechiel.) Qua in re pensandum est, cum omnis culpa munere solvatur, quam gravis est culpa discordiae, pro qua nec munus accipitur. Debemus itaque ad proximum, quamvis longe positum longeque disjunctum, mente ire, eique animum subdere, humilitate illum ac benevolentia placare, ut videlicet Conditor, dum tale munus nostrae mentis aspexerit, a peccato nos solvat, quia munus [Col. 0028B] pro culpa sumit. Veritatis autem voce testante didicimus, quia servus qui decem millia talenta debebat, cum poenitentiam ageret, absolutionem debiti a Domino accepit. Sed quia conservo suo centum sibi denarios debenti debitum non dimisit, et hoc est jussus exigi, quod ei fuerat jam dimissum. Ex quibus videlicet dictis constat, quia si hoc quod in nos delinquitur ex corde non dimittimus, et illud rursus exigitur, quod nobis jam per poenitentiam dimissum fuisse gaudebamus.
chunks.english:
[Gregory] In this matter we must consider this: if every fault is resolved by an offering, how serious must the fault of discord be, when for its sake even the offering is not accepted.

So we must go in our minds to our neighbor, even if that neighbor is far away and far removed from us. We must humble our heart before him and appease him with humility and goodwill. Then, when the Creator sees this kind of offering in our mind, he will release us from sin, because he accepts the offering in place of the fault.

We have learned from the voice of Truth himself that the servant who owed ten thousand talents received from his lord the cancellation of his debt when he repented. But because that servant did not forgive the debt of his fellow servant, who owed him one hundred denarii, he was ordered to pay again the very debt that had already been forgiven him.

From these words it is clear: if we do not forgive from the heart what has been done against us, then what we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance will be demanded from us again.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “GREG., homil. 8 in Ezechiel.” The biblical parable is alluded to without a printed citation; it refers to the unforgiving servant in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter eighteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 15. (S. CYPR.) Summopere autem necesse est, ut quando stamus ad orationem, quando tam sancta et veneranda mysteria sub oculis Dei geruntur, toto corde ad precandum invigilemus. Cogitatio omnis carnalis et saecularis abscedat, nec quidquam animus [Col. 0028C] quam id solum cogitet quod precatur. Ideo et sacerdos ante illam sacrosanctam orationem, praefatione praemissa, parat fratrum animos dicendo: «Sursum corda,» ut dum respondet: «Habemus ad Dominum,» admoneatur nihil aliud se quam Dominum cogitare debere, claudatur contra adversarium pectus, et soli Deo pateat, nec ad se adire hostem Dei tempore orationis patiatur. Obrepit enim frequenter et penetrat, et subtiliter fallens preces nostras a Deo avocat, ut aliud habeamus in corde, et aliud in voce, quando intentione sincera Deum non vocis sonus; sed animus et sensus debeat orare, quasi sit aliud quod magis cogitare debeamus, quam quod cum Deo loquimur. Quomodo a Deo audiri postulamus, cum nos ipsi non audiamus? Volumus esse Deum memorem [Col. 0028D] nostri, quando memores nostri ipsi non sumus, hoc est quando oramus, majestatem Dei negligentia orationis offendere, hoc est vigilare oculis et corde dormire, cum debeat Christianus, etiam dum dormit oculis, corde vigilare, sicut scriptum est ex persona Ecclesiae loquentis in Cantico canticorum: «Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat» (Cant. V, 2). Quapropter sollicite et caute Apostolus admonet dicens: «Instate orationi vigilantes in ea» (Col. IV, 2), docens scilicet et ostendens, eos impetrare quod postulant a Deo posse, quos ipse videt in oratione vigilare.
chunks.english:
[Cyprian] It is absolutely necessary that, when we stand for prayer, and when such holy and awe-inspiring mysteries are being carried out before the eyes of God, we keep watch in prayer with our whole heart. Every fleshly and worldly thought must go away. The mind must think of nothing except the very thing for which it is praying.

That is why, before that most holy prayer, the priest first gives the preface and prepares the hearts of the brethren by saying, “Lift up your hearts.” And when the people answer, “We have lifted them up to the Lord,” each person is being reminded that he must think of nothing but the Lord. His heart is to be closed against the adversary and open to God alone. He must not allow the enemy of God to come near him during the time of prayer.

For the enemy often creeps in and makes his way inside. By a subtle deception he draws our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another on our lips. Yet it is not the sound of the voice, but the mind and understanding, that should pray to God with sincere attention—as if there could be anything more important to think about than the fact that we are speaking with God.

How do we ask to be heard by God, when we ourselves do not even hear ourselves? We want God to remember us, while we ourselves do not remember ourselves. That is, when we pray carelessly, we offend the majesty of God by our neglect in prayer. We are awake with our eyes and asleep in our heart, although a Christian ought to keep watch with the heart even while sleeping with the eyes. As Scripture says, speaking in the person of the Church in the Song of Songs, chapter five, verse two: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.”

Therefore the Apostle gives this careful and watchful warning when he says in Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter four, verse two: “Persevere in prayer, keeping watch in it.” He is teaching and showing that those whom God sees keeping watch in prayer are able to obtain from God what they ask.
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: “(S. CYPR.)”. Column markers omitted from the English as editorial apparatus.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quid est ergo sursum habere corda, nisi ea quae sursum sunt quaerere, quae sursum sunt sapere? quaerere videlicet amando, sapere intelligendo, [Col. 0029A] sicut Apostolus eodem sermone admonet dicens: «Si consurrexistis cum Christo, quae sursum sunt quaerite, ubi Christus est in dextera Dei sedens; quae sursum sunt sapite, non quae super terram» (Col. III, 1). Hunc ascensum cordis nostri qui fit ad Deum a convalle plorationis, id est ab humilitate contribulationis, non nostris viribus, sed auxilio Dei ostendit nobis Psalmista dicens: «Beatus vir cujus est auxilium abs te, ascensiones in corde suo disposuit in valle lacrymarum» (Psal. LXXXIII, 6). Ascensus enim utilis non potest esse, nisi primo humilitatis a convalle nobis ascendendum esse meminerimus. Convallis enim locus est terrae depressus. Docens ipse Dominus a convalle plorationis ascendendum, quando pro nobis humiliari usque ad mortem crucis et pati [Col. 0029B] dignatus est. Hoc exemplum non relinquamus. Istam convallem plorationis martyres intellexerunt, et inde ut coronarentur ascenderunt. Amor sanctus ad superna elevat, et ad aeterna inflammat. Obligata enim anima amore terreno, quasi viscum habet in pennis, volare non potest; mundata vero ab affectibus sordidissimis saeculi, tanquam extensis pennis et duabus alis resolutis, id est duobus praeceptis dilectionis Dei et dilectionis proximi, volat ad Dominum, ascendens volando, quia ascendit amando ad illam scilicet supernam Jerusalem matrem omnium nostrum, quae est in coelis.
chunks.english:
So what does it mean to have our hearts lifted up, except to seek the things that are above and to set our minds on the things that are above? We seek them by loving them, and we set our minds on them by understanding them. In these very words the Apostle warns us in Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter three, verse one: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth.”

The Psalmist shows us that this ascent of our heart to God is made from the valley of weeping—that is, from the lowliness of affliction—not by our own strength, but with God’s help. He says in Psalm eighty-three, verse six: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears.”

No ascent can be useful unless we first remember that we must climb up from the valley of humility. A valley is a low place in the earth. The Lord himself teaches that we must ascend from the valley of weeping, since for our sake he was willing to be humbled even to death on a cross, and to suffer. Let us not abandon this example. The martyrs understood this valley of weeping, and from it they climbed up to receive their crowns.

Holy love lifts us toward the things above and sets us on fire for eternal things. A soul tied down by earthly love has, as it were, birdlime on its wings and cannot fly. But when it has been cleansed from the filthiest attachments of this world, then, like a bird with wings spread out and both wings freed—that is, with the two commandments of love of God and love of neighbor—it flies to the Lord. It rises by flying, because it rises by loving, toward that heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all, who is in heaven.
chunks.notes: Paul’s letter to the Colossians is cited as chapter three, verse one in the printed text, though the quotation also includes wording from verse two. Psalm numbering is rendered as printed: Psalm eighty-three, verse six.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Ab illa enim peregrinamur in hac vita, ad ejus reditum suspiramus tandiu miseri et laborantes, donec ad illam redeamus, nec cives nostri angeli dimiserunt in peregrinatione; [Col. 0029C] sed annuntiaverunt nobis ipsum regem venturum ad nos. Et venit ad nos, et contemptus est inter nos a nobis, et postea nobiscum, et docuit nos contemni, quia contemptus est; docuit tolerare, quia toleravit; docuit pati, quia passus est; et promisit resurrecturos, quia resurrexit, in seipso ostendens quid sperare debeamus. Si ergo prophetae et patres antiqui antequam Dominus Jesus Christus veniret in carne, antequam mortuus resurrexisset et ascendisset in coelum, suspirabant tamen illi civitati, quantum nos oporteat desiderare quo nos ipse praecessit, et unde nunquam recessit. Antiqui sacerdotes qui non tam curabant de cultu sermonis, quam de salute et aedificatione plebis, propter idiotas et rusticanos, non sursum, sed vulgari sermone «Sursum corda» dicere [Col. 0029D] solebant, ut res tanta planius omnium sensibus commendaretur. Monet autem adhuc sacerdos et dicit:
chunks.english:
From that city we are exiles in this life. We long to return to it, miserable and burdened as we are, until we do return. And our fellow citizens, the angels, have not abandoned us in our exile. Rather, they announced to us that the King himself would come to us.

And he did come to us. Among us he was despised by us, and afterward he was despised along with us. He taught us to accept being despised, because he himself was despised. He taught us to endure, because he endured. He taught us to suffer, because he suffered. And he promised that we would rise, because he rose, showing in himself what we ought to hope for.

So if the prophets and the ancient fathers, before the Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh, before he died, rose again, and ascended into heaven, still longed for that city, then how much more ought we to desire the place to which he himself has gone ahead of us, and from which he has never departed.

The priests of earlier times were not so concerned with polished speech as with the salvation and building up of the people. So, for the sake of the uneducated and the rural poor, they used to say the words “Lift up your hearts” not in their correct form but in the everyday pronunciation, so that so great a matter might be made clearer to everyone’s understanding.

The priest then continues his admonition and says:
chunks.notes: 'non sursum, sed vulgari sermone Sursum corda': Florus means the priests said the word in its colloquial form (probably 'susum') rather than the correct 'sursum'; the manuscript Zwettl 103 has an erased letter here (source apparatus, unresolved H04).

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 16. «Gratias agamus Domino Deo nostro.» Gratiarum actio Patri luminum semper a nobis debetur, a quo sine ulla dubitatione omne datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum, Scriptura teste, descendit. Nemo est enim donis Dei beatus, qui donanti exsistit ingratus, quia et hoc quod inter sacra mysteria cor habere sursum jubemur, ipso adjuvante id valemus, quod jubente admonemur. Et ideo sequitur, ut de hoc tanto bono sursum levati cordis non nobis gloriam, quasi nostrarum virium tribuamus, sed Domino Deo nostro gratias agamus. Hoc enim [Col. 0030A] continuo commonemur, quia hoc dignum est, hoc justum est; recordari oportet semper haec verba unde sint, inter quas actiones et quanta sanctitate commendentur, teneamus et habeamus quod accipimus, et datori gratias agamus. Quamvis enim accipere et habere nostrum sit, id tamen habemus quod accepimus, quoniam superbienti, et ex eo quod habebat, quasi a seipso haberet impie glorianti Veritas per Apostolum dicit: «Quid enim habes quod non accepisti; quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis?» (I Cor. IV, 7.) Merito ergo in illo verissimo et singulari sacrificio Domini, Deo nostro agere gratias admonemur, ut agnoscat homo, si quid bene vivit, Dei gratia se habere, et ut perficiatur in dilectione justitiae non se aliunde consecuturum, [Col. 0030B] quia cogitatio pium facit. Ipsa est illa sapientia quae pietas vocatur, qua colitur Pater luminum, a quo omne est datum optimum, et omne donum perfectum. Colitur autem sacrificio laudis actionibusque gratiarum, ut cultor ejus non in seipso, sed in illo glorietur. «Non enim spiritum hujus mundi accepimus,» ut ait idem Apostolus, «sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est» (I Cor. II, 12), ut sciamus quae a Deo donata sunt nobis. Quis est autem spiritus mundi hujus, nisi superbiae spiritus, quo cor insipiens obscuratum est eorum, qui cognitum Dominum, non ut Deum, gratias agendo glorificaverunt?
chunks.english:
“Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.”

Thanksgiving is always owed by us to the Father of lights, from whom, as Scripture bears witness, every good gift and every perfect gift undoubtedly comes down. No one is blessed by God’s gifts if he is ungrateful to the giver. For even this command—that during the sacred mysteries we are told to have our heart lifted up—we can carry out only with God’s help, just as we are reminded of it by God’s command.

And therefore it follows that, for so great a good as a heart lifted upward, we should not give glory to ourselves, as though it came from our own strength. Instead, we should give thanks to the Lord our God. We are immediately reminded that this is right and just. We must always remember where these words come from, amid what sacred actions they are commended to us, and with what great holiness. We should hold fast to what we receive, possess what we receive, and give thanks to the giver.

For although receiving and possessing are things we do, still what we possess is what we have received. To the proud person, who wickedly boasts about what he has as though he had it from himself, Truth speaks through the Apostle in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter four, verse seven: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

So rightly, in that most true and unique sacrifice of the Lord, we are reminded to give thanks to our God. Each person is to recognize that, if he lives rightly in any way, he has this by the grace of God; and that he will not obtain perfection in the love of righteousness from any other source. For this way of thinking is what makes a person devout. This is that wisdom called piety, by which the Father of lights is worshiped—the one from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes.

He is worshiped by the sacrifice of praise and by acts of thanksgiving, so that his worshiper may boast not in himself, but in him. As the same Apostle says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter two, verse twelve: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God,” so that we may know the things given to us by God.

And what is the spirit of this world, if not the spirit of pride? By that spirit, the foolish heart was darkened in those who knew the Lord, but did not glorify him as God by giving thanks.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Consideremus ergo haec, et de omnibus beneficiis Dei semper illi gratias referamus, interque omnia opera ejus, nihil est quod vel considerare libentius, vel laudare dulcius debeamus, quam [Col. 0030C] quod Christus factus est humilis, et ad hominem, qui cadendo ad ima dejectus fuerat, sponte descendit, ut vel sese erigendum crederet qui jacebat. Denique ut levaret in coelum spem nostram, levavit primo carnem nostram, et ut non dubitaremus secuturum quod promisit nobis, illuc iam praecessit quod accepit ex nobis.
chunks.english:
So let us consider these things, and let us always give thanks to him for all God’s benefits. And among all his works, there is nothing we should more gladly contemplate or more sweetly praise than this: Christ became humble, and freely came down to the human being who, by falling, had been cast down to the lowest depths, so that the one lying there might believe he could be raised up.

In short, to lift our hope to heaven, Christ first lifted our flesh to heaven. And so that we would not doubt that what he promised us would follow, what he received from us has already gone ahead of us to that place.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 17. (FULG., epist. 14, ad Ferrand., n. 44.) Ideo ergo praecipue in ipso sacrificio corporis Christi a gratiarum actione incipimus, ut Christum non dandum, sed datum nobis in veritate monstremus; et in eo quod gratias agimus Deo, in oblatione corporis et sanguinis Christi cognoscamus non adhuc occidendum Christum pro nostris iniquitatibus, sed occisum; nec redimendos nos illo sanguine, sed redemptos. [Col. 0030D] Vera est enim beati Petri praedicatio dicentis: «Non corruptibilibus argento vel auro redempti estis de vestra vana conversatione paternae traditionis; sed pretioso sanguine quasi Agni immaculati et incontaminati Christi» (I Petr. I, 18). Bene itaque admonenti sacerdoti et dicenti «Gratias agamus Domino Deo nostro,» respondet Ecclesia:
chunks.english:
[Fulgentius] Therefore, especially in the sacrifice of the body of Christ, we begin with thanksgiving in order to show the truth: Christ is not someone who is still to be given to us; he has already been given to us. And by giving thanks to God in the offering of the body and blood of Christ, we recognize that Christ is not still to be killed for our iniquities; he has already been killed. Nor are we still waiting to be redeemed by that blood; we have already been redeemed.

For the preaching of blessed Peter is true when he says in Peter’s first letter, chapter one, verse eighteen: “You were not redeemed from your vain way of life, handed down from your fathers, by corruptible silver or gold, but by the precious blood of Christ, like that of a spotless and undefiled lamb.”

So when the priest gives this good admonition and says, “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” the Church answers:
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: “(FULG., epist. 14, ad Ferrand., n. 44.)”. Peter’s first letter is cited as chapter one, verse eighteen in the printed text, though the quotation continues into verse nineteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 18. «Dignum et justum est.» Quid enim potest esse magis Deo dignum, aut quid ei justius a nobis rependi potest, quam et tantae misericordiae Dei, cui vicem referre non possumus, debitas gratias reddamus, audientes Apostolum exhortantem nos et dicentem: «Gratias agentes Deo et Patri, qui dignos»[Col. 0031A] «nos fecit in sorte sanctorum in lumine, qui eripuit nos de potestate tenebrarum, et transtulit in regnum Filii charitatis suae, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ejus, remissionem peccatorum?» (Col. I, 12, 13, 14.) Sic enim dilexit Deus mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret, et gratia Dei pro omnibus gustaret mortem. Qui ergo per hanc gratiam eripimur de potestate tenebrarum, id est diaboli et angelorum ejus, et transferimur in regnum Filii dilectionis Dei, ut efficiamur genus electum, regale sacerdotium, habentes in eodem Filio per sanguinem ejus redemptionem, remissionem peccatorum; quid dignius agere possumus, quam quod beatus Petrus apostolus admonet dicens: «Et virtutes annuntietis ejus, qui de tenebris vos vocavit in admirabile lumen suum; qui»[Col. 0031B] «aliquando non populus, nunc autem populus Dei, qui non consecuti misericordiam, nunc autem misericordiam consecuti?» (I Petr. II, 9.) Hanc ergo Ecclesiae responsionem confirmat sacerdos, et in Deum mente suspensus, cognoscente secum omni Ecclesia proclamat et dicit:
chunks.english:
“It is right and just.”

For what could be more worthy of God, or what could we more justly give back to him, than to offer the thanks we owe for so great a mercy of God—mercy that we cannot repay in kind? We hear the Apostle urging us when he says in Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter one, verses twelve through fourteen: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light; who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.”

For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, and by the grace of God he tasted death for all. Therefore, through this grace, we are rescued from the power of darkness—that is, from the devil and his angels—and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love, so that we may become a chosen race and a royal priesthood, possessing in that same Son, through his blood, redemption, the forgiveness of sins.

So what more worthy thing can we do than what the blessed apostle Peter urges when he says in Peter’s first letter, chapter two, verse nine: “Proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light; you who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; you who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy”?

The priest therefore confirms this response of the Church. With his mind lifted up to God, and with the whole Church joining in this acknowledgment, he proclaims and says:
chunks.notes: Peter’s first letter is cited as chapter two, verse nine in the printed text, though the quotation includes wording from verse ten.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 19. «Vere dignum et justum est, aequum et salutare.» Quod est justum, hoc est et aequum, sed repetitio sermonis, confirmatio est veritatis, nam justitia et aequitas una res est, sicut cantamus in psalterio de Domino: «Judicabit orbem terrae in justitia et populos in aequitate» (Psal. XCV, 10). Salutare autem dicitur, quod est salubre, et quod salutem conferat. Vere ergo ut incessanter gratias agamus, dignum est tantis Dei beneficiis, justum nostris obsequiis, aequum ipso pondere rationis, salutare manifesto fructu salutis, quo et Deum laudantes salvantur, et ingrati ipsius judicio reprobantur.
chunks.english: “It is truly right and just, equitable and saving.” What is just is also equitable. But repeating the idea strengthens the truth, because justice and equity are one reality. So we sing in the Psalter about the Lord: “He will judge the whole world in justice, and the peoples in equity,” from the Book of Psalms, Psalm ninety-five, verse ten. A thing is called “saving” when it is wholesome and brings salvation. So it is truly fitting that we should give thanks without ceasing: fitting because God’s benefits are so great; just because of the service we owe him; equitable by the very weight of reason; and saving by the evident fruit of salvation. For those who praise God are saved, while the ungrateful are rejected by his judgment.
chunks.notes: Section number omitted from the spoken translation as editorial numbering.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Nam Deum fideliter laudantes vere salvantur, sicut in psalmo cantatur: «Laudans invocabo Dominum et ab inimicis meis salvus ero» (Psal. XVII, 4). Ingrati autem reprobantur, sicut aperte in Evangelio ipse Dominus ostendit, qui ex decem leprosis ejus virtute mundatis, unum ad se suppliciter revertentem, et magna voce gratias agentem, laudavit, et gratia fidei salvavit, dicendo: «Non est inventus qui rediret et daret gloriam Deo, nisi hic alienigena;» et continuo clementer adjunxit: «Surge, vade, quia fides tua te salvum fecit» (Luc. XVII, 18).
chunks.english: For those who faithfully praise God are truly saved, as the Psalm says: “Praising, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies,” from the Book of Psalms, Psalm seventeen, verse four. But the ungrateful are rejected. The Lord himself shows this plainly in the Gospel. Ten lepers were cleansed by his power, yet only one returned to him in supplication and gave thanks with a loud voice. The Lord praised him and saved him by the grace of faith, saying: “No one was found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner.” And at once, in his mercy, he added: “Rise, go; your faith has made you well,” from the Gospel of Luke, chapter seventeen, verse eighteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Novem autem reliquos, licet crediderint se per eum posse mundari, quando una voce clamaverunt dicentes: «Jesu praeceptor, miserere nostri;» tamen quia tantae virtuti exstiterunt ingrati, velut infideles, nescire se ostendit, dicendo: «Nonne decem mundati sunt, et novem ubi sunt?» (Matth. XXV, 12.) Nescire autem Dei reprobari est: unde et quibusdam dicturus est: «Amen dico vobis, nescio vos.» Ex quo quantum malum sit gratiarum actionem Deo debitam negligere, evidenter ostenditur, quando eos quos credentes mundavit, etiam mundatos istius culpae merito tanquam infideles abjecit.
chunks.english: As for the other nine: they did believe that they could be cleansed through him, when they cried out together, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” Yet because they were ungrateful after such a mighty act, he showed that he did not know them, treating them like unbelievers, when he said: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” from the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-five, verse twelve. For God’s “not knowing” someone means that the person is rejected. That is why he will also say to some people: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” This shows clearly how grave an evil it is to neglect the thanksgiving owed to God: even those whom he cleansed when they believed, he afterwards cast aside as unbelievers because they were guilty of this fault, even though they had been cleansed.
chunks.notes: The printed citation “Matth. XXV, 12” is rendered as printed. The words “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine?” are actually from the Gospel of Luke, chapter seventeen, verse seventeen; Matthew chapter twenty-five, verse twelve corresponds to the later quotation, “I do not know you.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Gratias autem agere debemus semper et ubique, id est in omni tempore et in omni loco, ut impleatur in nobis quod cantamus in psalmo: «Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo» (Psal. XXXIII, 2). Et iterum: «In omni loco dominationis ejus benedic anima mea Domino» (Psal. CII, 22).
chunks.english: But we must give thanks always and everywhere—that is, at every time and in every place—so that what we sing in the Psalm may be fulfilled in us: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth,” from the Book of Psalms, Psalm thirty-three, verse two. And again: “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, my soul,” from the Book of Psalms, Psalm one hundred two, verse twenty-two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 20. (AUG., Enar. II in Psal. XXXIII, n. 4.) Quis est ergo qui benedicit et gratias agit Domino in omni tempore, nisi humilis corde? Ipsam enim humilitatem docuit Dominus noster in corpore suo, quia cum commendat corpus et sanguinem suum, humilitatem suam commendat. Esto humilis, si vis benedicere Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore tuo, quia et Job non tantum benedixit Dominum, quando abundabant illi omnia, quibus eum legimus divitem fuisse. Ablata sunt omnia uno tempore, et implevit quod in hoc psalmo scriptum est dicens: «Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit. Sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est.» Post: «Sit nomen Domini benedictum» (Job I, 21). Ecce habet exemplum benedicentis in omni tempore. Non habebat quae teneret, sed habebat quod laudaret. In laude Dei sui quasi in rerum copia quiescebat. Deus illi solatium fuit, ne possessionum damnis periclitaretur. Nunquid enim perdidit Deum, quamvis perdiderit quod dederat Deus?
chunks.english: [Augustine] So who is it who blesses the Lord and gives him thanks at all times, if not the one who is humble in heart? Our Lord taught this very humility in his own body, because when he entrusts to us his body and blood, he entrusts to us his humility. Be humble, then, if you want to bless the Lord at all times, with his praise always in your mouth. Job did not bless the Lord only when he had plenty of everything, during the time when, as we read, he was rich. Everything was taken from him all at once, and he fulfilled what is written in this Psalm when he said: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done.” Then he added: “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” from the Book of Job, chapter one, verse twenty-one. Here is an example of someone blessing God at all times. Job had nothing left to hold on to, but he still had someone to praise. He rested in the praise of his God as if he were resting in an abundance of possessions. God was his comfort, so that the loss of property would not destroy him. After all, had he lost God, even though he had lost what God had given?
chunks.notes: Printed source siglum: “(AUG., Enar. II in Psal. XXXIII, n. 4.)”. Section number omitted from the spoken translation as editorial numbering.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Plus est enim habere eum qui dat, quam illa quae dat. Si enim pulchra sunt quae dat, quanto pulchrior ille qui dat? Si magna sunt, quanto major ipse largitor? Et certe quae in hac terrena vita dederit Deus, aut dum vivimus nos deserunt, aut a nobis morte deseruntur. At vero ipse Deus aeterna possessio semper praesens nunquam deserit possidentem. Sint ergo casta vota fidelium, vilescat temporale bonum, et veniat aeternum. Inhaereat Deo anima pia in eum oratione suspensa, et per spirituales amplexus ei connexa desideret illud quod secum ipse largitur. Quantum est quod nobis exhibebit Deus, si seipsum nobis nolit exhibere? Si ergo bona suppetunt saeculi, sit misericordiae faciendae materies: si defuerint, sit patientiae fidelis occasio.
chunks.english: For it is better to possess the giver than to possess the things he gives. If the things he gives are beautiful, how much more beautiful is the one who gives them? If they are great, how much greater is the giver himself? And certainly, whatever God gives in this earthly life either leaves us while we are still living, or else we leave it behind at death. But God himself is an eternal possession, always present; he never abandons the one who possesses him. So let the desires of the faithful be pure. Let temporary goods become cheap in our eyes, and let the eternal good come. Let the devout soul cling to God, lifted up to him in prayer; joined to him in a spiritual embrace, let it desire what he gives together with himself. What would it amount to for God to give us something, if he were unwilling to give us himself? So if the goods of this world are available, let them become material for works of mercy. If they are lacking, let that become an opportunity for faithful patience.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Tali enim devotione etiam in omni loco Deo gratiae aguntur, quia qui ubique est praesens, ubique agnoscit laudatorem suum, etiam cum ore quiescente, et tacente lingua, secreto cordis affectu fidelis ei anima benedicit, cum agit in silentio quod canitur in psalmo: «Benedic, anima mea, Domino, et omnia quae intra me sunt nomini sancto ejus» (Psal. CII, 1). Quisquis ergo supplicaturus et gratias acturus Deo, locum sanctum et aptum requiris, interiora tua munda, et omni inde mala cupiditate depulsa, praepara tibi in cordis tui pace secretum, volens in templo orare. In te ora, et ita age semper, ut templum Dei sis. Ibi enim Deus exaudit, ubi habitat.
chunks.english: With devotion like this, thanks are given to God in every place as well. For the one who is present everywhere recognizes his worshiper everywhere. Even when the mouth is still and the tongue is silent, the faithful soul blesses him in the hidden affection of the heart, doing silently what is sung in the Psalm: “Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name,” from the Book of Psalms, Psalm one hundred two, verse one. So, if you are looking for a holy and suitable place in which to pray to God and give him thanks, cleanse your inner self. Drive out every evil desire from within, and prepare for yourself a hidden place in the peace of your heart, since you want to pray in a temple. Pray within yourself, and always live in such a way that you are God’s temple. For God hears prayer where he dwells.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 21. «Vere dignum et justum est, aequum et salutare nos tibi semper et ubique gratias agere.» Subjungit ad quem dirigat orationem dicendo: «Domine, sancte Pater omnipotens, aeterne Deus,» et per quem eamdem orationem dirigat addendo: «Per Christum Dominum nostrum.» Quod ergo dicit, «Domine,» refertur ad creaturae subjectionem, de quo et in psalmo canitur: «Quoniam omnia serviunt tibi» (Psal. XV, 1). Et alibi: «Dixi Domino: Deus meus es tu, quoniam bonorum meorum non eges.» Quid est enim «bonorum meorum,» nisi a te datorum? quomodo eget aliquo bono, a quo omne bonum datur? Ideo verus est Dominus, qui servo suo non indiget. Et quo servo indiget?
chunks.english: “It is truly right and just, equitable and saving, that we should give you thanks always and everywhere.” Next he adds to whom he directs the prayer, saying: “Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God.” And he adds through whom he directs that same prayer: “Through Christ our Lord.” So when he says “Lord,” this refers to the subjection of every creature. About this we sing in the Psalm: “For all things serve you,” from the Book of Psalms, Psalm fifteen, verse one. And elsewhere: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, for you have no need of my goods.” What are “my goods,” after all, except goods given by you? How could the one from whom every good is given need any good thing? Therefore he is the true Lord, because he has no need of his servant. And what servant would he need?
chunks.notes: Section number omitted from the spoken translation as editorial numbering. The printed citation “Psal. XV, 1” is rendered as printed. In the Vulgate tradition, “For all things serve you” is found elsewhere in the Psalms, while the following quotation, “I said to the Lord…,” corresponds to Psalm fifteen, verse two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quod vero adjungit «sancte Pater,» refertur vel specialiter ad unigeniti Filii generationem, in qua coaeternus et coaequalis Patri, de qua etiam Propheta ait: «Generationem ejus quis enarrabit?» (Isa. XXXV, 8) vel generaliter ad omnium filiorum Dei adoptionem, cujus tanta est gratia, ut cum haberet unicum, noluerit illum esse unum, sed ut fratres haberet, adoptavit illos qui cum illo possiderent vitam aeternam, pro quibus ipse eisdem verbis Patri supplicans ait: «Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo, quos dedisti mihi» (Joan. XVII, 11).
chunks.english: When he adds “holy Father,” this can refer in a special sense to the begetting of the only-begotten Son, in which the Son is co-eternal and co-equal with the Father. About this begetting the Prophet also says: “Who will tell of his generation?” from the Book of Isaiah, chapter thirty-five, verse eight. Or it can refer more generally to the adoption of all God’s children. The grace of this adoption is so great that, although God had one only Son, he did not want him to remain alone. Instead, so that his Son would have brothers, God adopted those who would possess eternal life together with him. Praying for them to the Father, the Son himself used these same words: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me,” from the Gospel of John, chapter seventeen, verse eleven.
chunks.notes: The printed citation “Isa. XXXV, 8” is rendered as printed. The quotation “Who will tell of his generation?” is normally associated with Isaiah chapter fifty-three, verse eight in the Vulgate tradition.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Haec ergo vox, ut dicatur Deo «Pater sancte,» et propria est unici Filii per naturam, et communis omnium adoptione filiorum per gratiam, per quam etiam concessit ut orantes dicant: «Pater noster, qui es in coelis» (Matth. VI, 9), qui vere omnipotens et aeternus est Deus, omnipotens scilicet virtute, qua omnia condidit et continet et regit, veraciter Scriptura dicit, «quia tibi impossibile nihil est.»
chunks.english: So this way of addressing God—calling him “holy Father”—belongs properly to the only Son by nature, and it belongs in common to all God’s adopted children by grace. Through that grace, he also allowed them to say in prayer: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” from the Gospel of Matthew, chapter six, verse nine. He is truly almighty and eternal God: almighty, that is, by the power with which he created all things, holds all things together, and governs all things. Scripture speaks truly when it says, “Nothing is impossible for you.”
chunks.notes: The final scriptural quotation has no citation in the printed Latin.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 22. (ID. ibid.) Qui tamen sic omnipotens est, ut nunquam suae rationis instituta convellat. Ipsius est etiam vera aeternitas, cui quod est esse perpetuum est, qui initio carens, sicut nullum finem, ita nullam recipit mutabilitatem. Tota autem oratio et gratiarum actio, quam semper et ubique debemus, dirigitur et offertur Deo Patri per Christum Dominum nostrum, tanquam per mediatorem et conciliatorem Dei et hominum, de quo Apostolus ait: «Unus enim»[Col. 0033C] «Deus, unus et mediator Dei et hominum homo Jesus Christus, qui dedit semetipsum redemptionem pro omnibus» (I Tim. II, 5), qui cum in natura deitatis sit unum cum Patre, suscipiendo naturam nostram, factus est nobis mediator ad Patrem. Ideo enim mediator Dei et hominum, quia Deus cum Patre, quia homo cum hominibus, non mediator homo praeter deitatem, non mediator Deus praeter humanitatem. Divinitas sine humanitate non est mediatrix, humanitas sine divinitate non est mediatrix. Sed inter solam divinitatem et humanitatem solam, mediatrix est humana divinitas, et divina humanitas Christi, qui etiam semetipsum obtulit in passione pro nobis, ut tanti capitis corpus essemus, secundum formam servi. Hanc enim obtulit, in hac [Col. 0033D] oblatus est, quia secundum hanc mediator est. In hac sacerdos, in hac sacrificium. Per ipsum ergo et petitiones et laudes suas offert Ecclesia Deo Patri, sciens per eum solum se posse accipere quod postulat, per eum solum placere posse quod laudat, sicut in Evangelio promittit dicens: «Amen, amen dico vobis, si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis» (Joan. XVI, 23). Haec est enim mediationis gratia per quam exauditur Ecclesia, secundum quam et Apostolus exhortatur dicens: «Per ipsum ergo offeramus hostiam laudis semper Deo» (Hebr. XIII, 15), id est fructum labiorum confitentium nomini ejus. Idem namque mediator Dei et hominum Deus super nos homo [Col. 0034A] propter nos per humanitatem interpellat pro nobis apud Patrem, per divinitatem exaudit et praestat cum Patre, sicut ipse testatur dicens: «Quia ego ad Patrem vado, et quodcunque petieritis in nomine meo hoc faciam, ut clarificetur Pater in Filio» (Joan. XIV, 12). De qua mediatione et advocatione etiam beatus Joannes apostolus ait: «Advocatum habemus apud Patrem Jesum Christum justum, et ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris» (I Joan. II, 2), quia qui per humanitatem interpellat pro nobis apud Patrem, idem per divinitatem propitiatur nobis cum Patre. Orat itaque sacerdos pro Ecclesia, orat Ecclesia pro sacerdote, sicut orat Apostolus pro plebe, orat plebs pro Apostolo, qui dicit: «Orantes simul et pro nobis, ut Deus aperiat nobis ostium verbi» (Coloss. IV, 3). [Col. 0034B] Et pro Petro orat Ecclesia cum esset in vinculis, quomodo et Petrus pro Ecclesia, quia omnia pro invicem membra orant. Caput pro omnibus interpellat, de quo scriptum est: «Qui et est ad dexteram Dei, aui etiam interpellat pro nobis» (Rom. VIII, 34).
chunks.english:
[Augustine] Yet God is almighty in such a way that he never tears apart the order established by his own reason. True eternity also belongs to him: for him, to be is to exist forever. Since he has no beginning, he has no end, and he admits no change.

All prayer and thanksgiving, which we owe always and everywhere, is directed and offered to God the Father through Christ our Lord, as through the mediator and reconciler of God and human beings. Of him the Apostle says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all”—Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse five.

Christ, who in the nature of his divinity is one with the Father, became our mediator with the Father by taking on our nature. He is mediator between God and human beings because he is God with the Father and human with human beings. He is not mediator as a human being apart from divinity, nor as God apart from humanity. Divinity without humanity is not the mediator; humanity without divinity is not the mediator. Rather, between divinity alone and humanity alone, the mediator is the human divinity and the divine humanity of Christ.

He also offered himself in his passion for us, so that we might become the body of so great a head, according to the form of a servant. This is what he offered; in this he was offered, because according to this human nature he is mediator. In this nature he is priest; in this nature he is sacrifice.

Through him, therefore, the Church offers its petitions and praises to God the Father. The Church knows that only through him can she receive what she asks, and only through him can the praise she offers be pleasing. As he promises in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you”—the Gospel of John, chapter sixteen, verse twenty-three.

This is the grace of mediation through which the Church is heard. In keeping with it, the Apostle urges us: “Through him, then, let us always offer to God a sacrifice of praise”—the letter to the Hebrews, chapter thirteen, verse fifteen—that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.

For the same mediator between God and human beings is God above us and human for our sake. Through his humanity he intercedes for us before the Father; through his divinity he hears and grants together with the Father. As he himself testifies: “Because I go to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, I will do this, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son”—the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, verse twelve.

About this mediation and advocacy, blessed John the Apostle also says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the atonement for our sins”—John’s first letter, chapter two, verse two. For the one who, through his humanity, intercedes for us before the Father is the same one who, through his divinity, is gracious to us together with the Father.

So the priest prays for the Church, and the Church prays for the priest, just as the Apostle prays for the people and the people pray for the Apostle. He says: “Praying also for us, that God may open for us a door for the word”—Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter four, verse three. And the Church prayed for Peter when he was in chains, just as Peter prayed for the Church, because all the members pray for one another. The Head intercedes for all, as it is written: “He is at the right hand of God, and he also intercedes for us”—Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verse thirty-four.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(ID. ibid.)”; rendered as [Augustine] on the assumption that it continues the preceding patristic source. The printed Latin has “aui etiam interpellat,” evidently for “qui etiam interpellat”; translated by sense and noted here. The citation to the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, verse twelve is spoken as printed, though the quoted wording also overlaps the following verse.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 23. (GREG. lib. XXII Moral., n. 42.) Unigenito enim Filio pro homine interpellare est apud coaeter num Patrem seipsum hominem demonstrare, eique pro humana natura rogasse, est eamdem naturam in divinitatis suae celsitudine suscepisse. Interpellat igitur pro nobis Dominus non voce, sed miseratione, quia quod damnari in electis noluit, suscipiendo servavit: qui quoniam hoc quod moriendo in sepulcro posuit, resurgendo super angelos elevavit; recte sacerdos adjungit et dicit:
chunks.english:
[Gregory] For the only-begotten Son to intercede for humanity means this: before the Father, who is coeternal with him, he shows himself as human. And to have pleaded for human nature means that he has taken that same nature up into the height of his own divinity.

So the Lord intercedes for us not by speaking aloud, but by showing mercy. What he did not want to be condemned in his chosen ones, he saved by taking it upon himself. And because the nature he laid in the tomb by dying, he raised above the angels by rising again, the priest rightly adds and says:
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(GREG. lib. XXII Moral., n. 42.)”.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0034C] 24. «Per quem majestatem tuam laudant angeli.» Haec est enim ineffabilis gloria Salvatoris et mediatoris nostri, qui, ut Apostolus ait, «purgationem peccatorum faciens, sedet ad dexteram majestatis in excelsis, tanto melior angelis effectus, quanto differentius prae illis nomen haereditavit» (Heb. I, 3). Cujus nominis altitudinem alibi exponens dicit: «Propter quod et Deus illum exaltavit, et donavit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, coelestium, terrestrium, et infernorum» (Phil. II, 9), quatenus per eumdem mediatorem laudet, adoret et contremiscat majestatem Dei Patris non solum Ecclesia hominum in terris, sed etiam Ecclesia angelorum in coelis.
chunks.english:
“Through whom the angels praise your majesty.”

This is the inexpressible glory of our Savior and mediator. As the Apostle says, “Having made purification for sins, he sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become so much greater than the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs”—the letter to the Hebrews, chapter one, verse three.

Explaining the height of that name elsewhere, the Apostle says: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth”—Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two, verse nine.

Thus, through this same mediator, not only the Church of human beings on earth, but also the Church of angels in heaven, praises, adores, and trembles before the majesty of God the Father.
chunks.notes: The phrase “Through whom the angels praise your majesty” is a liturgical lemma from the Preface. The citation to Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two, verse nine is spoken as printed, though the quotation continues into the following verse.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 25. (AUG., serm. CCCXL, n. 11.) Sic enim Ecclesia [Col. 0034D] tota et una accipienda est, non solum ex ea parte qua peregrinatur in terris a solis ortu usque ad occasum laudans nomen Domini, et post captivitatem vetustatis cantans canticum novum; verum etiam ex illa quae in coelis semper ex quo condita est cohaesit Deo, nec ullum malum sui casus experta est. Haec in sanctis angelis beata persistit, et suae parti peregrinanti sicut oportet opitulatur, quia utraque una erit consortio aeternitatis, et nunc vera est vinculo charitatis. Haec ergo quae peregrinatur in terris, sanguine Mediatoris nullum habentis peccatum, ab omni est peccato redempta,... ejus non est. «Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? qui Filio proprio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum» (Rom. VIII, 32). Non [Col. 0035A] enim pro angelis mortuus est Christus; sed ideo etiam pro angelis fit ipsa redemptio hominum, quoniam cum ipso redimus in gratiam post inimicitias quas inter homines et sanctos angelos peccata fecerunt, et ex ipsa hominum redemptione, ruinae illius angelicae damna reparantur. Propter hoc ait Apostolus, «instaurari omnia in Christo, quae in coelis sunt et quae in terris» (Eph. I, 10). In ipso instaurantur, quippe quae in coelis sunt, cum id quod inde in angelis lapsum est, hominibus redditur. Instaurantur autem quae in terris sunt, cum ipsi homines qui praedestinati sunt in aeternam vitam, a corruptionis vetustate renovantur, ac sic per illud singulare sacrificium, in quo mediator est immolatus, pacificantur coelestia cum terrestribus, et terrestria cum [Col. 0035B] coelestibus, quoniam sicut Apostolus dicit: «In ipso complacuit omnem plenitudinem habitare, et per eum reconciliari omnia in ipsum, pacificans per sanguinem crucis ejus sive quae in terris sunt, sive quae in coelis» (Col. I, 22). De ipso namque et alibi idem Apostolus ait: «Et ipse est caput corporis Ecclesiae» (Ib., vers. 18). Et iterum: «Et estis in illo repleti, qui est caput omnis principatus et potestatis» (Col. II, 10). Omnes ergo qui ab initio saeculi fuerunt justi, caput Christum habent. Illum enim venturum esse crediderunt, quem nos venisse jam credimus, et in ejus fide et ipsi sanati sunt, in cujus et nos, ut esset ipse totius caput civitatis Jerusalem omnibus connumeratis fidelibus ab initio usque in finem, adjunctis etiam legionibus et exercitibus angelorum, ut fiat una civitas [Col. 0035C] sub uno rege, et una quaedam provincia sub uno imperatore, felix in perpetua pace ac salute, laudans Dominum sine fine beato fine. Istorum vero trium ordinum spirituum, id est angelorum, dominationum, potestatum, qui divinam majestatem laudare, adorare, et tremere dicuntur, talis est differentia.
chunks.english:
[Augustine] The whole Church must be understood in this way as one: not only that part of the Church which is on pilgrimage on earth, praising the name of the Lord from the rising of the sun to its setting, and singing a new song after the captivity of the old life, but also that part which is in heaven. From the moment it was created, that heavenly part has always clung to God and has never suffered the evil of falling away.

This heavenly Church remains blessed in the holy angels, and it helps its pilgrim part as it ought. Both parts will be one in the shared life of eternity, and even now they are truly one by the bond of love.

So that part of the Church which is on pilgrimage on earth has been redeemed from every sin by the blood of the Mediator, who has no sin. Here a few words are missing from the printed Latin text. “If God is for us, who is against us? He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all”—Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verse thirty-two.

Christ did not die for the angels. Yet the redemption of human beings also benefits the angels, because through Christ we are restored to friendship with them, after the hostilities that human sins had created between human beings and the holy angels. And through this redemption of humanity, the losses caused by that angelic fall are repaired.

For this reason the Apostle says that “all things are restored in Christ, the things in heaven and the things on earth”—Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter one, verse ten. The things in heaven are restored in him when what fell from there among the angels is given back from among human beings. The things on earth are restored when those human beings who have been predestined to eternal life are renewed from the decay of the old condition.

And so, through that one unique sacrifice in which the mediator was sacrificed, heavenly things are reconciled with earthly things, and earthly things with heavenly things. As the Apostle says: “In him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or the things in heaven”—Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter one, verse twenty-two.

About him, the same Apostle says elsewhere: “And he is the head of the body, the Church”—Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter one, verse eighteen. And again: “And you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power”—Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter two, verse ten.

Therefore all the righteous who have existed from the beginning of the world have Christ as their head. They believed that he would come; we believe that he has already come. They were healed in the same faith in which we too are healed. Thus Christ is the head of the whole city of Jerusalem, with all the faithful counted together from beginning to end, and with the legions and armies of angels joined to them. There will be one city under one king, like one province under one emperor, happy in everlasting peace and salvation, praising the Lord without end, in a blessed end.

As for those three orders of spirits—that is, angels, dominions, and powers—who are said to praise, adore, and tremble before the divine majesty, this is the difference among them.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(AUG., serm. CCCXL, n. 11.)”. The phrase “redempta,... ejus non est” is corrupt or lacunose in the printed Latin; it has been represented explicitly in the English rather than silently repaired. The citation to Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter one, verse twenty-two is spoken as printed, though the quotation corresponds more closely to Colossians chapter one, verses nineteen through twenty. “Ib., vers. 18” has been expanded in English as Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter one, verse eighteen.  Printed text 'et nunc vera est vinculo charitatis' (Augustine's text reads 'una'); rendered 'truly one' as the evident sense (cross-family review r07-01).

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 26. (GREG., hom. 34 in Evang., n. 8 et seq.) Quod angeli, qui Latine «nuntii» interpretantur, ex ipso nomine officium suum nobis indicant, quia videlicet a Deo missi, voluntatem ejus hominibus nuntiant, sicut legimus in Veteri Testamento missos angelos ad Abraham, ad Loth, ad Jacob, ad Moysen, ad Josue, ad Daniel et Tobiam, et in Novo frequenter, unde et per Psalmistam dicitur: «Benedicite Domino»[Col. 0035D] «angeli ejus, potentes virtute, facientes verbum illius, ad audiendum vocem sermonis ejus» (Psal. CII, 29). Et iterum: «Qui facit angelos suos spiritus» (Psal. CIII, 4), ac si aperte dicat, qui eos quos semper habet spiritus, etiam cum voluerit angelos, id est nuntios facit. Dominationes autem vocantur et angelorum agmina, quae mira potentia praeeminent, eo quod eis caetera ad obediendum subjecta sint. Potestates etiam vocantur hi qui hoc potentius caeteris in suo ordine perceperunt, ut eorum ditioni virtutes adversae subjectae sint, quorum potestate refrenantur, ne corda hominum tantum tentare praevaleant, quantum volunt. Hi ergo tam beati et sublimes in coelestibus spiritus per Christum Dominum nostrum majestatem Dei [Col. 0036A] laudant, sicut ad eos gratulando dicitur in psalmo: «Laudate Dominum de coelis, laudate eum in excelsis. Laudate eum, omnes angeli ejus, laudate eum virtutes ejus» (Psal. CXLVIII, 1). De quibus et Deus in libro Job loquitur dicens: «Quando facta sunt sidera, laudaverunt me omnes angeli mei voce magna» (Job XXXVIII, 7). Adorant quoque eamdem divinam majestatem, sicut in hymno confessionis Esdrae ad ipsum Deum dicitur: «Tu ipse, Domine Deus, qui fecisti coelum, coelum coeli et universa quae in eo sunt, et tu vivificas omnia haec, et exercitus coeli te adorant» (II Esd. IX, 6). Tremunt etiam sicut per figuram de eis in libro Job dicitur: «Columnae coeli contremiscunt, et pavent ad nutum ejus» (Job XXVI, 10).
chunks.english:
[Gregory] Angels—translated into Latin as “messengers”—show us their office by their very name. They are sent by God and announce his will to human beings. In the Old Testament, we read of angels sent to Abraham, to Lot, to Jacob, to Moses, to Joshua, to Daniel, and to Tobias; and in the New Testament this happens often.

So the Psalmist says: “Bless the Lord, his angels, mighty in strength, doing his word, ready to hear the voice of his speech”—Psalm one hundred two, verse twenty-nine. And again: “He makes his angels spirits”—Psalm one hundred three, verse four.
