It is as if Scripture were saying plainly: the ones whom God always has as spirits, he also makes angels—that is, messengers—whenever he wills.

Dominions are those companies of angels that stand out with wondrous power, because the other spirits are subject to them in obedience. Powers are those who, in their own order, have received this with greater strength than the others: hostile powers are subject to their authority and are restrained by their power, so that they cannot tempt human hearts as much as they would like.

These blessed and exalted spirits in heaven, then, praise the majesty of God through Christ our Lord. The psalm joyfully addresses them: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers”—Psalm one hundred forty-eight, verse one.

God also speaks of them in the book of Job, saying: “When the stars were made, all my angels praised me with a loud voice”—Job, chapter thirty-eight, verse seven. They also adore the same divine majesty, as the hymn of confession in Esdras says to God: “You yourself, Lord God, made heaven, the heaven of heaven, and everything in it; you give life to all these things, and the host of heaven adores you”—Second Esdras, chapter nine, verse six. They also tremble, as is said figuratively of them in the book of Job: “The pillars of heaven tremble and are afraid at his nod”—Job, chapter twenty-six, verse ten.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(GREG., hom. 34 in Evang., n. 8 et seq.)”. The citation “Psalm one hundred two, verse twenty-nine” is spoken as printed, though the quoted line corresponds to Psalm one hundred two, verse twenty in the Vulgate numbering. In the Vulgate tradition, “Second Esdras” often corresponds to Nehemiah; the English keeps the printed reference. The citation “Job, chapter twenty-six, verse ten” is spoken as printed, though the quoted wording corresponds to Job chapter twenty-six, verse eleven in many editions.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 27. (ID., lib. XVII Mor., n. 44.) Quia ipse quoque [Col. 0036B] virtutes coelestium quae Deum sine cessatione conspiciunt, in ipsa sua contemplatione contremiscunt. Sed iisdem timor ne eis poenalis sit, non timoris est, sed admirationis. Cum igitur in coelestibus tanta sit devotio laudantium, veneratio adorantium, tremor admirantium, consideret haec homo, cui dictum est: «Quid superbit terra?» et audiat Apostolum monentem: «Cum metu et timore et tremore vestram ipsorum salutem operamini» (Phil. II, 12). Sequitur sacerdos in Dei laudibus, et dicit:
chunks.english: [Gregory] For even the powers of heaven, who look upon God without ceasing, tremble in the very act of contemplating him. But for them this fear is not a punishment; it is not terror, but wonder. So, since among the heavenly beings there is such devotion in praise, such reverence in worship, and such trembling in wonder, let the human being consider this—the human being to whom it was said, “Why is earth proud?” And let him listen to the Apostle’s warning: “Work out your own salvation with fear, reverence, and trembling”—Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two, verse twelve. The priest continues in the praises of God and says:
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(ID., lib. XVII Mor., n. 44.)”, referring back to Gregory. The quotation “Quid superbit terra?” is given without a biblical citation in the printed text.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 28. «Coeli coelorumque virtutes ac beata Seraphim socia exsultatione concelebrant.» Subauditur hoc quod jam supradictum est, «majestatem tuam.» Hanc namque non solum, ut praemissum est, angeli, dominationes, et potestates laudant, adorant, tremunt; [Col. 0036C] sed etiam coeli, et coelorum virtutes, et Seraphim concelebrant, id est in commune celebrant, concordi devotione et communi gaudio laudant. Nam celebritas est conventus populi in laude, et celebrata dicimus in celebri, id est in frequentissimo conventu acta. Celebrat itaque et concelebrat majestatem Dei beatus ille populus angelorum, de cujus inenarrabili multitudine scriptum est: «Millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies centena millia assistebant ei» (Dan. VII, 10), quia adest illis semper vultus praesens Dei, dicente Domino in Evangelio: «Angeli eorum in coelis semper vident faciem Patris mei qui in coelis est» (Matth. XVIII, 10). Qui dum sine defectu conspicitur et amatur, amatur et laudatur, electorum civium mera laetitia agitur, vicissim de se omnes in [Col. 0036D] suo conventu gratulantur. Ipsa est enim domus Dei aeterna, de qua in Psalmis canitur: «Beati qui habitant in domo tua, in saecula saeculorum laudabunt te» (Psal. LXXXIII, 5). Et iterum: «Sicut laetantium omnium habitatio est in te» (Psal. LXXXVI, 7). Ideo hic bene dicitur, quia majestatem Dei socia, id est juncta exsultatione concelebrant, quoniam, ut jam dictum est, sine intermissione laudantes vicissim de illo, et de se in illo laetantur, sicut de ipsis Seraphim manifeste in Isaia legitur, «quia volabant alter ad alterum, et dicebant, Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus,» etc. (Isa. VI, 3).
chunks.english: “The heavens, the Virtues of the heavens, and the blessed Seraphim celebrate it together with shared exultation.” We should understand the words already mentioned: they celebrate “your majesty.” For, as was said above, not only angels, dominions, and powers praise, adore, and tremble before that majesty; the heavens, the Virtues of the heavens, and the Seraphim also celebrate it together—that is, they celebrate it in common, praising it with one devotion and one shared joy. A “celebration,” after all, means an assembly of people gathered in praise; and we call things “celebrated” when they are done in a crowded, public assembly. So that blessed people of the angels celebrates, and celebrates together, the majesty of God. Scripture says of their indescribable multitude: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten times a hundred thousand stood before him”—the book of Daniel, chapter seven, verse ten. For the face of God is always present to them, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven”—the Gospel of Matthew, chapter eighteen, verse ten. Since God is seen without failing and loved without failing, he is loved and praised; the citizens he has chosen live in pure joy, and in their assembly they all rejoice with one another. This is the eternal house of God, of which the Psalms sing: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever”—Psalm eighty-three, verse five. And again: “The dwelling of all who rejoice is in you”—Psalm eighty-six, verse seven. So it is well said here that they celebrate God’s majesty together with shared—that is, united—exultation. As has already been said, they praise him without interruption, and they rejoice together over him and over themselves in him. This is clearly read about the Seraphim themselves in Isaiah: “They flew, one toward another, and said, ‘Holy, holy, holy,’” and so on—the book of Isaiah, chapter six, verse three.
chunks.notes: The Isaiah quotation is translated as printed: “volabant alter ad alterum,” “they flew, one toward another.” In the standard biblical text of Isaiah chapter six, verse three, the wording is “they cried one to another,” while “they flew” appears nearby in the same vision.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 29. (AUG.) Merito enim laudant cui ministrant, et assistunt, et dant gloriam in excelsis Deo, quia illi [Col. 0037A] debent quod sunt, illi debent quod vivunt, illi debent quod juste vivunt, illi debent quod beate vivunt, ne putemus hominem solum pertinere ad gratiam Dei. Quid erat angelus antequam fieret? quid est angelus si deserat qui creavit? Hunc ergo omnium creatorem laudant et concelebrant coeli, sicut eum laudant sol et luna, omnes stellae et lumen. Unde in psalmo dicitur: «Laudate eum sol et luna; laudate eum omnes stellae et lumen. Laudate eum coeli coelorum, et aquae omnes quae super coelos sunt laudent nomen Domini» (Psal. CXLVIII, 3).
chunks.english: [Augustine] They rightly praise the one whom they serve, before whom they stand, and to whom they give glory in the highest. For to him they owe what they are; to him they owe that they live; to him they owe that they live rightly; and to him they owe that they live blessedly. We must not think that only human beings depend on the grace of God. What was an angel before he was made? And what is an angel if the one who created him abandons him? Therefore the heavens praise and celebrate this Creator of all things, just as the sun and moon praise him, and all the stars and light. Hence the Psalm says: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let all the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord”—Psalm one hundred forty-eight, verse three.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(AUG.)”. The printed citation gives Psalm one hundred forty-eight, verse three, though the quotation also includes material corresponding to the following verse in the Psalm.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 30. (AUG.) In hymno quoque trium puerorum ad laudem Dei elementa omnia provocantur, non quod elementa muta habeant sensum laudandi; sed quia cuncta bene cogitata laudem pariant, et impletur [Col. 0037B] cor consideratione creaturae ad eructandum hymnum Creatori. Et quia longum fuit in ista gratiarum actione totos angelorum ordines, qui in Scripturis novem inveniuntur, sigillatim ponere; post coelos ponuntur Virtutes, quo nomine omnes coelestes spiritus nonnunquam generaliter appellari solent, ut est illud in psalmo: «Verbo Domini coeli firmati sunt, et spiritu oris omnis virtus eorum» (Psal. XXXI, 6). Et iterum: «Dominus virtutum ipse est rex gloriae» (Psal. XXIII, 10). Tamen proprie in ordinibus angelorum Virtutes illi spiritus vocantur, per quos signa et miracula frequentius fiunt. Ad ultimum ponuntur seraphim, qui est summus ordo angelicorum spirituum; et vere beata, quae ex singulari propinquitate conditoris sui incomparabili ardent amore. Unde et Seraphim «ardentes» [Col. 0037C] vel «incendentes» interpretantur: quia quo subtilius claritatem divinitatis aspiciunt, eo validius in ejus amore flammescunt.
chunks.english: [Augustine] Likewise, in the hymn of the three young men, all the elements are summoned to praise God—not because the mute elements have a conscious power to praise, but because everything, when rightly considered, gives rise to praise, and the heart is filled by contemplating creation until it pours out a hymn to the Creator. And because, in this thanksgiving, it would have been too long to list one by one all the orders of angels—of which nine are found in Scripture—the Virtues are named after the heavens. This name, “Virtues,” is sometimes used in a general way for all the heavenly spirits, as in the Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power”—Psalm thirty-one, verse six. And again: “The Lord of powers, he is the king of glory”—Psalm twenty-three, verse ten. Strictly speaking, however, among the orders of angels, the Virtues are those spirits through whom signs and miracles are most often done. Last of all the Seraphim are named. They are the highest order of angelic spirits, and they are truly blessed, because, from their uniquely close nearness to their Creator, they burn with an incomparable love. This is why “Seraphim” is interpreted as “burning ones” or “those who set on fire”: the more subtly they gaze upon the brightness of the Godhead, the more strongly they blaze with love for him.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(AUG.)”. The first Psalm citation is printed as Psalm thirty-one, verse six; the quoted text corresponds to Psalm thirty-two, verse six in the Vulgate numbering, and Psalm thirty-three, verse six in many modern English Bibles. “Virtutes” can mean both “powers” and “virtues”; here it is rendered “Powers” when referring to the angelic order.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 31. (VIGIL.) Sciendum quoque quod cherubim et seraphim per «m» litteram prolata, juxta proprietatem linguae Hebraeae, masculini sunt generis et pluralis numeri tantum. Si autem per «n» litteram dicantur, sicut in psalmis et hymnis, et in praesenti gratiarum actione ponitur, Graeca declinatione in neutrale genus mutantur, velut cum dicimus lucida sidera, speciosa nemora, jucunda littora: sic et beata seraphin neutrali genere et plurali numero accipimus. Illud autem attentissime cognoscendum, quod ante ita sancti angeli et caeterae coelorum virtutes majestatem [Col. 0037D] Dei Patris laudare, tremere, et communi exsultatione concelebrare dicuntur per Christum Dominum nostrum, tanquam haec venerationis et glorificationis obsequia soli Deo Patri deferant, non etiam Filio et Spiritui sancto. Certissima enim fide tenere et scire debemus, quia totius sanctae Trinitatis. Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti, sicut una est divinitas et individua majestas, ita ei in omnibus aequalis honor et individua glorificatio debetur; nec ullo modo aut Pater sine Filio, aut Filius sine Patre et Spiritu sancto aut laudari, aut adorari, aut ullo divini cultus obsequio honorari potest.
chunks.english: [Vigilius] We should also know that “Cherubim” and “Seraphim,” when pronounced with the letter em at the end, are, according to the proper usage of Hebrew, masculine in gender and only plural in number. But if they are pronounced with the letter en at the end, as happens in psalms and hymns and in the present thanksgiving, then by Greek declension they are changed into the neuter gender. It is like when we say, in Latin, “bright stars,” “beautiful groves,” or “pleasant shores”: in the same way, we understand “blessed Seraphin” as neuter in gender and plural in number. But we must recognize this very carefully: earlier, the holy angels and the other powers of heaven were said to praise, tremble before, and celebrate with shared exultation the majesty of God the Father, through Christ our Lord. This should not be understood as though they offered these acts of veneration and glorification to God the Father alone, and not also to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Rather, we must hold and know with absolute faith that, just as there is one divinity and one undivided majesty of the whole holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so also equal honor and undivided glorification are due to the Trinity in all things. In no way can the Father be praised, adored, or honored with any service of divine worship without the Son; nor can the Son be praised, adored, or honored without the Father and the Holy Spirit.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(VIGIL.)”. The discussion turns on Latin grammatical endings: “Seraphim” and “Cherubim” with final m, versus “Seraphin” and “Cherubin” with final n. The English translation preserves the distinction by naming the final letters explicitly.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 32. (VIGIL.) Nulla enim est in Trinitate distantia; sed sive quis Patrem adoret, ibi est Filius et Spiritus [Col. 0038A] sanctus. Sive Filio et Spiritu sancto supplicet, ibidem sine dubio et Pater invenitur, quia dum Patrem aut Filium invocas, totam Deitatis unitatem, totam amplecteris Trinitatem. Si enim vere et fideliter creditur, quia Pater in Filio et Filius in Patre est, sicut Isaias ad eumdem Filium loquitur dicens: «In te est Deus, et non est Deus praeter te» (Isa. XLV, 14). Et in Evangelio: «Ego,» inquit, «in Patre et Pater in me est» (Joan. X, 38), nulli dubium, quod similiter ut Patri etiam Filio, qui in eodem Patre consubstantialiter manet, a nobis sacrificium immoletur. Cum enim ita in se invicem, ut separari nequeant manent, quod uni exhibueris, utrisque exhibitum crede. Denique Filius ait: «Qui me vidit vidit et Patrem. Ego et Pater unum sumus» (Joan. XIV, 9), sic visio Filii Patris est [Col. 0038B] contemplatio, Patris honorificentia sive gloria, dicente eodem Filio, ut omnes honorificent Filium, sicut honorificant Patrem.
chunks.english: [Vigilius] For there is no separation within the Trinity. If someone adores the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are there. If someone prays to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, the Father is certainly found there as well. For when you invoke the Father or the Son, you embrace the whole unity of the Godhead, the whole Trinity. If we truly and faithfully believe that the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father—as Isaiah says, speaking to that same Son, “God is in you, and there is no God besides you”—the book of Isaiah, chapter forty-five, verse fourteen—and as he says in the Gospel, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me”—the Gospel of John, chapter ten, verse thirty-eight—then there is no doubt that the sacrifice is offered by us to the Son as well as to the Father, since the Son remains in that same Father as one of the same substance. For since they remain in one another in such a way that they cannot be separated, believe that whatever you offer to one is offered to both. Finally, the Son says: “Whoever has seen me has also seen the Father. I and the Father are one”—the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, verse nine. Thus the vision of the Son is the contemplation of the Father; and honoring the Son is the honor or glory of the Father, as the same Son says, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: “(VIGIL.)”. The final printed citation is the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen, verse nine. The first sentence quoted there matches that reference; the second, “I and the Father are one,” corresponds to the Gospel of John, chapter ten, verse thirty. The Latin prints only the one citation, and it is rendered as printed.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 33. (AUG.) Quid si inveniuntur qui Patrem honorificant, et non honorificant Filium? Non potest, inquit, fieri. Qui non honorificat Filium, non honorificat Patrem qui misit illum; sed ne forte Patrem quidem honorifices tanquam majorem, Filium vero tanquam minorem, corrigit te ipse Filius et revocat te dicens, ut omnes honorificent Filium non inferius, sed sicut honorificant Patrem. Quidquid ergo mandatis coelestibus obsequendo divinitati exhibemus, sive in sacrificiorum ritu, sive in supplicatione precum, sive in alio quolibet munificentiae genere et Patri et Filio aequaliter debetur, ac si nullum venerationis honorem privatim possidet Pater, qui non ad Filii et Spiritus sancti pertineat dignitatem. Nam si sacramentum regenerationis baptisma ad eos aequaliter pertinet, dum in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus sancti beata illa secundae nativitatis gratia celebratur; nulli dubium quod et mysteriorum sacrificia communi dignitatis honore Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus possidet, quia inseparabili Deitatis unitate Trinitas ipsa connexa est.
chunks.english: [Augustine] What if there are people who honor the Father, but do not honor the Son? He says: that cannot happen. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. But in case you try to honor the Father as greater, and the Son as lesser, the Son himself corrects you and calls you back, saying that everyone must honor the Son—not with a lower honor, but just as they honor the Father. So whatever we offer to the divine majesty in obedience to heavenly commands—whether in the rite of sacrifices, or in prayers of supplication, or in any other kind of generous service—is owed equally to the Father and to the Son. The Father possesses no private honor of veneration that does not also belong to the dignity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For if baptism, the sacrament of regeneration, belongs equally to them, since that blessed grace of the second birth is celebrated in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, then no one should doubt that the sacrifices of the mysteries also belong to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit by one shared honor of dignity, because the Trinity itself is joined together in the inseparable unity of the Godhead.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: (AUG.). Column marker omitted from English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Ut autem ad solum Patrem oratio dirigatur, id apostoli sancti, sancto per eos ordinante Spiritu, sanxerunt, ut qui multorum deorum errores unius Dei praedicatione nitebantur evellere, sub Trinitatis sacramento uni personae in sacrificiorum ritu supplicandum esse decernerent, ne qui unum Deum, ob falsorum deorum exstirpandos errores, praedicabant, in pluralem divinitatis numerum incidisse arguerentur ab his qui ineffabile Patris et Spiritus sancti mysterium ignorabant. Rectissime ergo constitutum est, ut quia Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus unius Deitatis, unius naturae, unius aequalitatis, unius denique potestatis exsistunt, una ex eis persona propter unitatis mysterium retinendum in sacrificio invocarentur. Nec alia debuit, nisi quae prima est, in qua caeterae duae naturaliter manentes exsistunt.
chunks.english: But the holy apostles, with the Holy Spirit ordering this through them, established that prayer should be directed to the Father alone in this way. They were trying, by preaching the one God, to tear out the errors of many gods. Therefore, while preserving the mystery of the Trinity, they decided that in the rite of sacrifice supplication should be made to one person, so that those who preached one God in order to root out the errors of false gods would not be accused—by people who did not understand the inexpressible mystery of the Father and the Holy Spirit—of having fallen into a plurality of gods. It was therefore most rightly established that, since the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one Godhead, one nature, one equality, and finally one power, one person among them should be invoked in the sacrifice, so that the mystery of unity might be maintained. And it should be no other person than the first, the Father, in whom the other two persons exist, naturally abiding.
chunks.notes: The phrase “the first” refers to the Father as the first person of the Trinity, not to any priority in time or superiority of nature. Column marker omitted from English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quod vero per Filium invocamus, cum ad eum dicimus: «Per Jesum Christum Filium tuum,» hic, ut supra jam dictum est, ex ea parte percipitur, qua pro nobis sacerdotis officio functus est, Tunc cum Deo Patri immaculatam suae carnis hostiam in ara crucis obtulit, unde vas electionis, «Considerate,» inquit, «apostolum et pontificem confessionis nostrae Jesum, qui fidelis est ei qui fecit eum» (Heb. III, 1). Factus ergo sacerdos pro nobis interpellet necesse est; sed ea, ut diximus, parte qua hominis gerit naturam. Unde et apostolus non divinitati, sed humanitati ejus hoc intercessionis ejus mysterium coaptavit dicens: «Unus enim mediator Dei et hominum homo Jesus Christus» (I Tim. II, 3).
chunks.english: As for the fact that we invoke the Father through the Son, when we say to him, “Through Jesus Christ your Son,” this is to be understood, as was said earlier, in relation to the role by which the Son performed the office of priest for us. That was when he offered to God the Father the spotless victim of his own flesh on the altar of the cross. Hence the chosen vessel says, “Consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to the one who made him,” in the letter to the Hebrews, chapter three, verse one. Therefore, since he was made priest for us, he must intercede for us; but he does this, as we have said, in the respect in which he bears human nature. That is why the apostle attached this mystery of Christ’s intercession not to his divinity, but to his humanity, when he said, “For there is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus,” in Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse three.
chunks.notes: The citation to the letter to the Hebrews is printed as chapter three, verse one, though the wording “who is faithful to the one who made him” continues into verse two in many biblical divisions. The citation to Paul’s first letter to Timothy is printed as chapter two, verse three; the quoted words correspond to chapter two, verse five in standard numbering.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quod autem oratio et adoratio sicut Patri, ita etiam et Filio deferatur, ostendit Isaias dicens: «Ipsum gentes deprecabuntur, et erit nomen ejus gloriosum» (Isa. XI, 10). Et iterum ubi inducit Deum Patrem loquentem ad Filium, «labor Aegyptiae, negotiatio Aethiopiae et Sabaim, viri sublimes, ad te transibunt, et tui erunt. Post te alligabunt» «vinculis alligati, et te adorabunt, teque deprecabuntur, quoniam in te est Deus, et non est praeter te» (Isa. XLV, 14). Item in Joel: «Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini salvus erit» (Joel. II, 32): quod de Filio dictum apostolus edocet tunc, cum Judaeorum incredulitatem exprobans ait: «Omnis qui invocaverit nomen Domini salvus erit. Quomodo invocabunt eum, in quem non crediderunt?» (Rom. X, 13). David etiam supremarum sedium confessorem Filium deprecans ait: «Qui sedes super cherubim, appare coram Ephraim, Benjamin, et Manasse. Excita potentiam tuam et veni, et salvos facias nos» (Psal. LXXIX, 3).
chunks.english: That prayer and adoration are offered to the Son just as they are to the Father is shown by Isaiah, who says, “The nations will pray to him, and his name will be glorious,” in the book of Isaiah, chapter eleven, verse ten. And again, where he introduces God the Father speaking to the Son, he says, “The labor of Egypt, the trade of Ethiopia and of the Sabaeans, lofty men, will pass over to you and will be yours. They will walk after you, bound in chains; and they will adore you and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no God apart from you,” in the book of Isaiah, chapter forty-five, verse fourteen. Likewise in Joel: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved,” in the book of Joel, chapter two, verse thirty-two. The apostle teaches that this was said about the Son when, reproaching the unbelief of the Jews, he says, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter ten, verse thirteen. David too prays to the Son, the one confessed as seated on the highest thrones, when he says, “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come, and save us,” in Psalm seventy-nine, verse three.
chunks.notes: Column marker omitted from English. The citation to Paul’s letter to the Romans is printed as chapter ten, verse thirteen, though the second quoted sentence continues into verse fourteen in standard numbering.  Isaiah 45:14: printed 'alligabunt' is an evident corruption of the Vulgate 'ambulabunt'; rendered 'will walk' (cross-family review r09-01). Printed 'confessorem' (David prays to the Son 'supremarum sedium confessorem') is probably a corruption of 'consessorem' (sharer of the throne); the English keeps a rendering of the printed word (cross-family review r09-02).

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Audi etiam Spiritum sanctum quemadmodum laudis sacrificium et Filio, et Patri, et sibi praecipit immolari, ubi vere individua Trinitas cum personarum distinctione evidentius demonstratur. Dicit ergo idem Spiritus sanctus in psalmo: «Immola Deo sacrificium laudis, et redde Altissimo vota tua, et invoca me in die tribulationis tuae, et eripiam te, et honorificabis me» (Psal. XLIX, 14). Ecce Spiritus sanctus et Deo Filio sacrificium laudis et Patri altissimo vota ac sibi invocationis et glorificationis hostiam a veritatis cultoribus suadet exhiberi.
chunks.english: Listen also to the Holy Spirit, and hear how he commands the sacrifice of praise to be offered to the Son, to the Father, and to himself. Here the truly undivided Trinity is shown more clearly together with the distinction of the persons. The same Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your trouble, and I will rescue you, and you will glorify me,” in Psalm forty-nine, verse fourteen. See, then: the Holy Spirit urges worshipers of the truth to offer the sacrifice of praise to God the Son, vows to the Most High Father, and to himself the offering of invocation and glorification.
chunks.notes: The citation is printed as Psalm forty-nine, verse fourteen; the words “call upon me…” continue into verse fifteen in many biblical divisions.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 34. (AUG.) De illo quippe dicit Apostolus: «Nescitis quia corpora vestra templum in vobis est Spiritus sancti, quem habetis a Deo et non estis vestri: quia empti estis pretio magno, glorificate et portate Deum in corpore vestro» (I Cor. VI, 15). Quemnam Deum nisi Spiritum sanctum, cujus corpora nostra esse dixerat templum?
chunks.english: [Augustine] For the apostle says about him: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple within you of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Glorify and carry God in your body,” in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verse fifteen. What God does he mean, if not the Holy Spirit, whose temple he had said our bodies are?
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: (AUG.). The citation is printed as Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verse fifteen; the quoted text corresponds chiefly to chapter six, verses nineteen through twenty in standard numbering.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 35. (VIGILIUS.) Debetur ergo gloria Spiritui sancto. Quod vero Virtutes angelicae cum Patre simul etiam Filium laudent atque glorificent, ostenditur nobis in Deuteronomio, ubi ita ad Filii venerationem coelestis invitatur exercitus: «Laetamini, coeli, simul cum eo, et adorent eum omnes angeli Dei. Laetamini, gentes, cum populo ejus, et glorificent eum omnes filii Dei.» In Apocalypsi quoque beatus Joannes postquam vidit quatuor animalia et viginti quatuor seniores eoram Agno, qui librum signatum aperuit, cecidisse dicentes: «Dignus es accipere librum et aperire signacula ejus, quoniam occisus es, et redemisti nos Deo in sanguine tuo,» subjunxit voces militiae coelestis redemptioni nostrae congratulantes, et ait: Et «vidi et» «audivi vocem angelorum multorum in circuitu throni, et erat numerus eorum millia millium dicentium voce magna, dignus est Agnus qui occisus est accipere virtutem et divinitatem et sapientiam et fortitudinem et honorem et gloriam et benedictionem» (Apoc. V, 9-12).
chunks.english: [Vigilius] Glory, then, is owed to the Holy Spirit. And that the angelic Powers praise and glorify the Son together with the Father is shown to us in Deuteronomy, where the heavenly army is invited to venerate the Son in this way: “Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God adore him. Rejoice, nations, with his people, and let all the sons of God glorify him.” Likewise in the Book of Revelation, blessed John first saw the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down before the Lamb, who had opened the sealed book, saying, “You are worthy to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood.” Then he added the voices of the heavenly host rejoicing over our redemption, and said: “And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing,” in the Book of Revelation, chapter five, verses nine through twelve.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: (VIGILIUS.). The Latin prints “eoram Agno,” evidently for “coram Agno”; translated as “before the Lamb.” The Deuteronomy quotation is introduced without a verse reference in the source, so no verse number is supplied. Column marker omitted from English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Post haec, inquit, «vidi, et ecce multitudo magna, quam dinumerare nemo poterat ex omni gente et tribu et populo et lingua stantes ante thronum et in conspectu Agni, amicti stolis albis, et palmae in manibus eorum, et clamabant voce magna dicentes: Salus Deo nostro sedendi super thronum, et Agno» (Apoc. VII, 9, 10). Ecce laudis sacrificium indiscrete Patri et Filio sanctorum immolat chorus, quorum voces multitudo angelorum adorando, et «amen» respondendo, confirmat, sicut statim in eodem libro sequitur: «Et omnes angeli» «stabant in circuitu throni, et ceciderunt in conspectu throni in facies suas, et adoraverunt Deum dicentes: Amen» (Ibid., vers. 11). Sanctum quoque Spiritum in eadem gloriae sublimitate beatus Petrus praedicat dicens: «Spiritui sancto misso de coelis, in quem desiderant angeli prospicere.» Sequitur sacerdos et dicit:
chunks.english: After this, he says, “I saw, and behold, a great multitude, which no one could count, from every nation and tribe and people and language, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands. And they cried out with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb,” in the Book of Revelation, chapter seven, verses nine through ten. See how the choir of saints offers the sacrifice of praise without distinction to the Father and to the Son. The multitude of angels confirms their voices by adoring and by answering, “Amen,” just as the same book immediately continues: “And all the angels stood around the throne, and they fell on their faces before the throne and adored God, saying: Amen,” in the Book of Revelation, chapter seven, verse eleven. Blessed Peter also proclaims the Holy Spirit in the same height of glory when he says, “The Holy Spirit sent from heaven, into whom the angels long to gaze.” The priest then continues and says:
chunks.notes: The printed “Ibid., vers. 11” has been resolved in English as the Book of Revelation, chapter seven, verse eleven. The Latin prints “sedendi super thronum,” translated according to the evident sense as “who sits upon the throne.” The quotation from Peter is given without a verse reference in the source, so no verse number is supplied.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 36. «Cum quibus et nostras voces, ut admitti jubeas deprecamur.» (GREG., lib. II Moral., n. 10.) Voces angelorum sunt in laude conditoris ipsa admiratio intimae contemplationis, quales ergo oportet esse voces nostras, quas in conspectu Dei cum angelicis laudibus deprecamur admitti, id est intromitti, ut possimus dicere: «Intret in conspectu tuo.» Et iterum; «ut veniat ad te oratio mea ad templum sanctum tuum.» Utique tales voces et talis clamor non est in sono oris, sed in desiderio cordis. Voces enim apud secretissimas aures Dei non faciunt verba nostra, sed desideria. Aeternam etenim vitam si ore petimus, nec tamen desideramus, clamantes tacuimus. Si vero desideramus ex corde, etiam cum ore conticescimus, tacentes clamamus. Sic Moyses ab strepitu verborum lacebat, et tamen silens aure divinae pietatis audiebatur, cur dicitur: «Quid clamas ad me?» (Exod. XIV, 15). Intus est ergo in desiderio clamor secretus, qui ad humanas aures non pervenit, et tamen auditum Conditoris replet;
chunks.english: “Together with them, we pray that you command our voices also to be admitted.” [Gregory] The voices of the angels, in praise of the Creator, are their very wonder in inward contemplation. So what kind of voices must ours be, when we pray that they may be admitted—that is, brought in—before God together with the praises of the angels? We should be able to say, “Let it enter into your sight.” And again: “Let my prayer come to you, to your holy temple.” Certainly voices of this kind, and a cry of this kind, do not consist in the sound of the mouth, but in the desire of the heart. For in the most hidden ears of God, it is not our words that make our voices, but our desires. If we ask for eternal life with our mouth, but do not desire it, then even while crying out we are silent. But if we desire it from the heart, then even when we are silent with the mouth, we cry out in silence. In this way Moses was silent, without the noise of words; and yet, while silent, he was heard by the ear of divine mercy. That is why it is said to him, “Why do you cry out to me?” in the book of Exodus, chapter fourteen, verse fifteen. So inwardly, in desire, there is a hidden cry. It does not reach human ears, and yet it fills the hearing of the Creator.
chunks.notes: Printed siglum: (GREG., lib. II Moral., n. 10.). The opening liturgical lemma is quoted exactly as printed. The Psalm-like phrases “Let it enter into your sight” and “Let my prayer come to you, to your holy temple” have no printed citations in the source, so none are supplied. The Latin prints “Moyses ab strepitu verborum lacebat”; translated according to the evident sense, probably “tacebat,” “was silent.” Column marker omitted from English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: et quia superna illa civitas ex angelis et hominibus constat, ad quam tantum credimus hominum genus ascendere, quantos illic contigit electos angelos remansisse, sicut scriptum est: «Statuit terminos gentium juxta numerum angelorum Dei,» merito sancta Ecclesia, quae illis socianda est in coelo, et cum illis in Dei laudibus permansura, jam nunc ipsis vocibus Deum laudat in terris, quibuscum sancti angeli laudant in coelis, et hoc non superba praesumptione, sed supplici confessione, et sic desiderans majestatem Dei credere et confiteri in mundo sicut ab angelis videtur, et laudatur in coelo. Haec enim confessio non est peccati, de qua nobis praecipitur: «Confitemini alterutrum peccata vestra» (Jac. V, 16). Et Psalmista ait: «Dixi: Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam» (Psal. XXXI, 5), sed laudis et gratiarum actionis, qualis intelligitur in psalmo ubi canimus: «Confiteantur Domino misericordiae ejus,» «et mirabilia ejus filiis hominum» (Psal. CVI, 8). Et qualem Dominus Jesus, qui nullum omnino habebat peccatum, in Evangelio Deo Patri offert dicens: «Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine coeli et terrae, quia abscondisti haec a sapientibus et revelasti ea parvulis» (Matth. XI, 23). Una igitur confessione, id est laude et gratiarum actione, jam nunc cum angelis sociantur, laudantes de coelestibus et terrestribus tanquam qui fecit coelum et terram dicentes.
chunks.english: And because that heavenly city is made up of angels and human beings, and because we believe that the human race will ascend to it in a number equal to the elect angels who remained there, as Scripture says, “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” the holy Church is right to praise God already now on earth with the very voices with which the holy angels praise him in heaven. For the Church is to be joined with them in heaven and to remain with them in the praises of God. It does this not with proud presumption, but with humble confession, desiring to believe in and confess the majesty of God in this world as it is seen and praised by the angels in heaven. This confession is not the confession of sin, about which we are commanded, “Confess your sins to one another,” in the letter of James, chapter five, verse sixteen. And the psalmist says, “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself,” in Psalm thirty-one, verse five. Rather, it is the confession of praise and thanksgiving, as we understand it in the Psalm where we sing, “Let them confess the mercies of the Lord, and his wonders to the children of men,” in Psalm one hundred six, verse eight. It is the kind of confession that the Lord Jesus, who had no sin at all, offers to God the Father in the Gospel when he says, “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter eleven, verse twenty-three. Therefore, through one confession—that is, through praise and thanksgiving—they are already now joined with the angels, praising God concerning heavenly and earthly things, as the one who made heaven and earth, and saying:
chunks.notes: The quotation “He established the boundaries…” is given without a printed biblical reference in the source, so no verse number is supplied. The citation to the Gospel of Matthew is printed as chapter eleven, verse twenty-three; the quoted words correspond to chapter eleven, verse twenty-five in standard numbering. The final “saying:” leads into the next liturgical text in the following chunk.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 37. «Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Dominus Deus sabaoth, pleni sunt coeli et terra.» Istae sunt voces angelorum laudantium in coelis hunc hymnum gloriae Dei. Et Isaias propheta se audisse testatur, quando gloriam Dei vidit, et seraphim istis vocibus eum collaudantia audivit. Et beatus Joannes in Apocalypsi sub [Col. 0041B] figura quatuor animalium introducit. Legitur namque in Isaia de seraphim laudantibus ita: «Et clamabant alter ad alterum, et dicebant: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus, Dominus Deus sabaoth, plena est omnis terra gloria ejus» (Isa. VI, 3). In Apocalypsi vero de quatuor animalibus sic legitur: «Et requiem non habebant, die ac nocte dicentia: Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Dominus Deus omnipotens, qui est, et qui erat, et qui venturus est» (Apoc. IV, 8).
chunks.english: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth, heaven and earth are full.” These are the words of the angels in heaven as they sing this hymn of God’s glory. The prophet Isaiah testifies that he heard them when he saw the glory of God and heard the seraphim praising him together with these words. And blessed John, in Revelation, presents the same praise under the figure of the four living creatures. For in Isaiah we read this about the seraphim as they give praise: “And they cried out, one to another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory”—the book of Isaiah, chapter six, verse three. But in Revelation we read this about the four living creatures: “And they had no rest, day or night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who is, and who was, and who is to come”—the book of Revelation, chapter four, verse eight.
chunks.notes: The opening liturgical quotation is printed without “gloria tua,” “of your glory,” though Florus discusses that phrase immediately below; translated as printed. Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Manifestum est ergo quod in his verbis divinae laudis, quae ad imitationem supernarum virtutum juxta Isaiam decantat Ecclesia, unus sermo de Apocalypsi additus sit: nam in Isaia tantum «Dominus sabaoth» legitur; in Apocalypsi vero «Dominus Deus omnipotens,» et ideo non humano arbitrio, sed utriusque Scripturae auctoritate conjuncta [Col. 0041C] dicimus: «Dominus Deus sabaoth.» Item in Isaia legitur: «Plena est omnis terra gloria ejus,» tanquam hoc angeli non ad ipsum Deum, sed de ipso ad invicem dicant, nos autem conversa ad eum voce dicimus: «Pleni sunt coeli et terra gloria tua:» quod non humano sensu praesumptum, sed de alia Scriptura assumptum et additum est, loquente ipso Deo in Jeremia propheta et dicente: «Coelum et terram ego impleo.» Quidquid autem in Dei laudibus Scriptura dicit, recte et ad ipsum dicitur gratulando, et de ipso ad alios exhortando vel instruendo.
chunks.english: So it is clear that, in these words of divine praise—which the Church sings in imitation of the heavenly powers, following Isaiah—one word has been added from Revelation. In Isaiah we read only, “Lord Sabaoth”; but in Revelation we read, “Lord God Almighty.” Therefore, it is not by human choice, but by the joined authority of both Scriptures, that we say: “Lord God Sabaoth.” Likewise, in Isaiah we read, “The whole earth is full of his glory,” as though the angels were saying this not directly to God, but to one another about him. But we turn our voice toward him and say: “Heaven and earth are full of your glory.” This too is not something presumed by human opinion; it is taken and added from another Scripture, where God himself speaks through the prophet Jeremiah and says: “I fill heaven and earth.” And whatever Scripture says in praise of God may rightly be said both to God himself, in joyful thanksgiving, and about God to others, in exhortation or instruction.
chunks.notes: Column marker omitted from the English. The Jeremiah quotation is printed without a chapter-and-verse citation, so none has been supplied.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 38. (HIERON.) Sabaoth autem est de decem nominibus Dei apud Hebraeos, et latine interpretatur exercituum, sive virtutum, sicut frequenter in prophetis positum est: «Haec dicit Dominus exercituum.» Et [Col. 0041D] in psalmo: «Dominus virtutum ipse est rex gloriae» (Ps. XXIII, 10). Qui ideo Dominus exercituum et Dominus virtutum vere dicitur, quia omnis militia coelestis exercitus, omnes supernae virtutes atque angelicae potestates ejus imperio subjacent, ejus serviunt voluntati.
chunks.english: [Jerome] Now Sabaoth is one of the ten names of God among the Hebrews. In Latin it is translated “of armies,” or “of powers,” as it is often used in the prophets: “Thus says the Lord of armies.” And in the Psalm: “The Lord of powers, he is the King of glory”—Psalm twenty-three, verse ten. He is truly called Lord of armies and Lord of powers because every host of the heavenly army, all the powers above and the angelic authorities, are subject to his command and serve his will.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(HIERON.)”. Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 39. (GREG., lib. XVII Mor., n. 19.) Angelicos enim spiritus recte militiam dicimus, quia decertare eos contra potestates aerias non ignoramus: quae tamen certamina non labore, sed imperio peragunt, quia quod agendum contra immundos spiritus appetunt ex adjutorio cuncta regentis possunt. De hac namque [Col. 0042A] militia nascente Rege nostro scriptum est: «Subito facta est cum angelo multitudo militiae coelestis» (Luc. III, 13).
chunks.english: [Gregory] We rightly call the angelic spirits an army, because we know that they fight against the powers of the air. Yet they carry out these battles not by toil, but by command, because whatever they desire to do against unclean spirits, they are able to do through the help of the one who governs all things. For of this army, when our King was born, it is written: “Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army”—the Gospel of Luke, chapter three, verse thirteen.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(GREG., lib. XVII Mor., n. 19.)”. The printed citation gives the Gospel of Luke, chapter three, verse thirteen; the quotation corresponds to Luke chapter two, verse thirteen. The citation has been spoken as printed. Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 40. (AMBR.) Quid sibi ergo vult in hoc hymno angelico sub uno nomine sanctitatis trina repetitio? Si trina repetitio, cur una laudatio? si una laudatio, cur trina repetitio, nisi quia Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus sanctitate unum sunt? Non dixit semel, ne Filium sequestraret; non bis, ne Spiritum sanctum praeteriret; non quater, ne creaturam conjungeret; et ut ostenderet unam esse Deitatem, cum tertio dixisset «sanctus, sanctus, sanctus,» addidit singulariter «Dominus sabaoth.» Sanctus igitur Pater, sanctus Filius, sanctus et Dei Spiritus, tota videlicet Trinitas adoratur et laudatur ab angelis. Hanc [Col. 0042B] seraphim glorificant et omnes potestates virtutesque coelestes. Adjungunt autem huic hymno angelorum sumpta ex Evangelio verba turbarum laudantium Deum et regem nostrum venientem Hierosolymam, atque dicentium:
chunks.english: [Ambrose] What, then, is the meaning, in this angelic hymn, of the threefold repetition of the one word “holy”? If it is repeated three times, why is there only one praise? And if there is only one praise, why is it repeated three times—unless because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in holiness? It was not said once, lest the Son be set apart. It was not said twice, lest the Holy Spirit be passed over. It was not said four times, lest a creature be joined to them. And to show that there is one Godhead, after saying for the third time, “Holy, holy, holy,” it adds in the singular, “Lord Sabaoth.” Therefore the Father is holy, the Son is holy, and the Spirit of God is holy; that is, the whole Trinity is adored and praised by the angels. The seraphim glorify this Trinity, as do all the heavenly authorities and powers. And to this hymn of the angels they add words taken from the Gospel: the words of the crowds praising God and our King as he came to Jerusalem, saying:
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(AMBR.)”. Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 41. «Hosanna in excelsis, benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini, hosanna in excelsis.» Ita enim ex Scriptura prophetica et evangelica completur plena laudatio, cum post laudem et gloriam sanctae Trinitatis adjungitur etiam gratiarum actio de adventu Salvatoris, qui unus in ipsa et ex ipsa Trinitate pro salute nostra homo factus in mundum venit, et eamdem salutem moriendo et resurgendo perfecit. «Mortuus est enim propter delicta nostra, et resurrexit propter justificationem nostram» (Rom. XIV, 25). Unde rite [Col. 0042C] illi gratias agentes, dicimus «Hosanna,» id est salus in excelsis.
chunks.english: “Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.” In this way the full praise is completed from prophetic and Gospel Scripture: after the praise and glory of the holy Trinity, thanksgiving is also added for the coming of the Savior. He, who is one within the Trinity and from the Trinity, became human and came into the world for our salvation; and he brought that same salvation to completion by dying and rising again. “For he died for our offenses, and rose again for our justification”—Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter fourteen, verse twenty-five. Therefore, giving thanks to him rightly, we say “Hosanna,” that is, salvation in the highest.
chunks.notes: The printed citation gives Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter fourteen, verse twenty-five; the quotation corresponds to Romans chapter four, verse twenty-five, and Romans chapter fourteen has no verse twenty-five in the usual numbering. The citation has been spoken as printed. Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: 42. (VIGILIUS.) Hoc est enim quod in psalmo canitur: «Domini est salus, et super populum tuum benedictio tua» (Ps. III, 9). Hoc quod in magnae devotione laudis in Apocalypsi sanctorum chorus resonat: «Salus Deo nostro, qui sedet super thronum, et Agno» (Apoc. VII, 10). Recte quoque subjungimus: «Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini,» juxta quod in Evangelio Judaeis non credentibus dixit: «Ego veni in nomine Patris mei, et non recepistis me» (Joan. V, 45), assumunt autem versiculum laudis turbae de psalmo centesimo decimo septimo, quem de Domino cantatum esse manifestum est: quod cum turbae dicunt hosanna, hoc est quod ibi dicitur: «O Domine, salvum»[Col. 0042D] «me fac! o Domine, bene prosperare!» et statim subjungitur: «Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini» (Ps. CXVII, 25).
chunks.english: [Vigilius] For this is what is sung in the Psalm: “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people”—Psalm three, verse nine. This is what the choir of the saints resounds in Revelation, in the devotion of great praise: “Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb”—the book of Revelation, chapter seven, verse ten. We also rightly add, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” in keeping with what he said in the Gospel to the unbelieving Jews: “I came in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me”—the Gospel of John, chapter five, verse forty-five. The crowds take up this little verse of praise from Psalm one hundred seventeen, which is clearly sung about the Lord. When the crowds say “Hosanna,” it is the same as what is said there: “O Lord, save me! O Lord, give good success!” And immediately it adds: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord”—Psalm one hundred seventeen, verse twenty-five.
chunks.notes: Full printed siglum: “(VIGILIUS.)”. The printed citation to the Gospel of John gives chapter five, verse forty-five; the quoted wording corresponds to John chapter five, verse forty-three. The citation has been spoken as printed. In the Psalm citation, the “Blessed is he” line is normally Psalm one hundred seventeen, verse twenty-six in the Vulgate, while the printed reference gives verse twenty-five; the citation has been spoken as printed. Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Quod vero in ejusdem laudis persecutione subjungitur «Hosanna,» id est salus sive salvifica in excelsis, aperte docet adventum Domini in carne, non solum humani generis in terra, sed et angelorum in coelis esse salutem: quia dum nos tendenti ad superna perducimur, eorum profecto numerus, qui Satana cedente erat minoratus, impletur. Hinc etenim Paulus ait: «Instaurari omnia Christo, quae in coelis et quae in terra sunt in ipso» (Ephes. I, 10). Recte igitur «Hosanna in altissimis» in ejus laude canitur, [Col. 0043A] cujus tota incarnationis dispensatio pro implenda gloria patriae coelestis apparuit.
chunks.english: And when, in the continuation of that same praise, “Hosanna” is added—that is, salvation, or saving power, in the highest—it openly teaches that the Lord’s coming in the flesh is salvation not only for the human race on earth, but also for the angels in heaven. For as we are brought upward toward the things above, the number of the angels, which had been diminished when Satan fell away, is surely filled up. Hence Paul says: “All things are restored in Christ, the things in heaven and the things on earth in him”—Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter one, verse ten. Therefore “Hosanna in the highest” is rightly sung in praise of him, since the whole saving plan of his incarnation appeared in order to complete the glory of the heavenly homeland.
chunks.notes: The printed Latin reads “in ejusdem laudis persecutione,” literally “in the persecution of the same praise.” I have translated the evident sense, “in the continuation of that same praise”; the likely intended reading is “prosecutione.” Column marker omitted from the English.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Post has laudes et gratiarum actiones, pro tanta gratia redemptionis nostrae, quae in illo divino mysterio agitur et commendatur, facto totius Ecclesiae silentio, in quo cessante omni strepitu verborum, sola ad Deum dirigatur intentio, et devotio cordium, sociatis sibi omnium votis et desideriis, incipit sacerdos orationem fundere, qua ipsum mysterium Dominici corporis et sanguinis consecratur. Sic enim oportet, ut in illa hora tam sacrae et divinae actionis, tota per Dei gratiam a terrenis cogitationibus mente separata et Ecclesia cum sacerdote et sacerdos cum Ecclesia spiritali desiderio intret in sanctuarium Dei supernum et aeternum. Et quoniam «Spiritus est Deus, et eos qui»[Col. 0043B] «adorant eum in spiritu et veritate oportet adorare» (Joan. IV, 24). Nam et Pater tales quaerit, qui adorent eum, sic eumdem Deum Patrem deprecetur, et dicat.
chunks.english: After these praises and thanksgivings for the great grace of our redemption—which is enacted and commended in that divine mystery—the whole Church falls silent. All noise of words ceases, so that only the mind’s attention and the devotion of hearts may be directed to God. Then, joining to himself the prayers and desires of all, the priest begins to pour out the prayer by which the mystery itself of the Lord’s body and blood is consecrated. For this is fitting: at that hour of so sacred and divine an action, by God’s grace the whole mind is separated from earthly thoughts, and the Church with the priest, and the priest with the Church, enter by spiritual desire into the heavenly and eternal sanctuary of God. And because “God is spirit, and those who adore him must adore in spirit and truth”—the Gospel of John, chapter four, verse twenty-four—and because the Father seeks such people to adore him, the priest prays to that same God the Father in this way, and says:
chunks.notes: Column marker omitted from the English. The final clause introduces the next prayer of the Mass.
